Latest Update: Your enterprise AI access can be sold for pennies – beware ‘LLM Mixers’

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (844 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in just a few years, businesses have adopted AI and large language models (LLMs) to manage everything from calendar invites to data analysis and programming.
  • Google’s latest report on AI threats, the Q4 AI Threat Tracker from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), found that gateways called LLM Mixers are selling access for cents on the dollar.
  • Also: 6 essential strategies to defend against AI-powered threat actors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in just a few years, businesses have adopted AI and large language models (LLMs) to manage everything from calendar invites to data analysis and programming. Bad actors steal credentials for those models through LLMjacking — and the marketplace is evolving.

Google’s latest report on AI threats, the Q4 AI Threat Tracker from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), found that gateways called LLM Mixers are selling access for cents on the dollar.

Also: 6 essential strategies to defend against AI-powered threat actors.

Organizations have poured billions of dollars into AI development and deployment, although the amount they spend on AI tokens every month varies. According to Ramp AI index data, among firms paying for AI, the top 1% spent over $10,000 per employee per month, compared with around $16 for the median firm. When employees have access to AI models, companies may introduce spending caps, but smaller outfits may overlook them.

According to recent reports, LLMjacking is the theft of AI-related credentials, including usernames and passwords, or API keys, used to access AI models. This gives cybercriminals the opportunity to use tokens and AI resources belonging to a victim organization (or individual), typically with usage-based billing or subscriptions with no fixed cap.

With these credentials, an unauthorized user could run high-resource computing tasks, manage their own malicious AI deployments, extract and steal corporate data from the AI’s memory, or even poison training data. To add insult to injury, if demand outstrips the limits of the victim’s subscription, cybercriminals can rack up high usage costs that the victim is then on the hook for.

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

John Hultquist, chief analyst for GTIG, previously stated the cybersecurity unit has seen a “major increase” in LLMjacking over 2026, so we can assume this trend will likely continue into 2027 and beyond.

AI access is now a lucrative illegal business in its own right, leading to what Google calls LLM Mixers: “illicit storefronts” that provide unauthorized access to AI services and underlying proxy infrastructure.

After analyzing LLMJacking vendor advertisements on Russian- and Chinese-language marketplaces, GTIG researchers found that most offer access not only to frontier models from AI labs, but also to jailbroken models marketed as suitable for malicious purposes.

However, it doesn’t seem that many of these cybercriminal groups can agree on “reasonable” pricing, with prices swinging wildly depending on the models offered and the credentials available.

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac – with Claude Code standing guard.

In a recent development, free trial credentials fetch far less than enterprise credentials, as you would expect. Token prices for business use ranged from $0.10 to $25, and one vendor, APIMart, increased its token price fivefold once a prompt exceeds 100,000 tokens. Other vendors offer subscription-based pricing.

This might not seem like much at the lower tiers, but Sysdig estimates LLMJacking could cost around $46,000 based on earlier models, and even over $100,000 per day on cutting-edge models. Mandiant research published earlier this month recorded incidents with illicit AI usage exceeding $100,000 in only 24 hours, with cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1 million before access was revoked.

While direct credentials can be sold, the infrastructure element is also an interesting service offering. Google’s threat team noted in the report that the sale of LLM infrastructure “routes buyer traffic through a pool of stolen credentials and compute instances to ensure reliable access, while also offering the ability to spread query volume across multiple victim environments to reduce the likelihood of detection.”.

In a recent development, LLM Mixers look similar to the rest of the cybercriminal underground economy, in which traders tend to specialize in one or two parts of an attack chain. For example, an LLM Mixer offers the access and infrastructure needed to exploit an enterprise AI model, while its partners might break into victim networks to secure initial access or buy stolen credentials from operators of infostealer malware.

Avoid LLMjacking and having your organization’s AI added to a Mixer’s menu similarly to how you would prevent intrusions into SaaS applications and cloud setups: managing access, monitoring, and imposing restrictions.

It has been revealed that usage and spending are the first areas to tackle. By setting limits on how many tokens can be issued and used across every AI service and account, and by alerting when usage suddenly spikes, organizations can limit damage if an account is compromised and stop massive bills before they rack up.

Also: Can you still trust Proton?

Organizations should also try to prevent their keys from ending up in the hands of cyberattackers in the first place. Google recommends using a secrets manager that securely stores and frequently rotates API keys, and running audits to detect quiet probing, misconfigurations, or shadow accounts.

It’s also advisable, across the board, to implement phishing protections and multi-factor authentication (MFA) to make the business of stealing credentials or compromising your accounts and networks more difficult in the first place.

  • Also: Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now.
  • The newly introduced remote lock feature is designed to work in tandem with other Microsoft services, such as Intune and BitLocker, to manage a fleet of devices both in-office and remotely across the globe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft is testing a upcoming feature that lets IT admins instantly lock down your lost or stolen device via remote connection, protecting your work projects and personal data from theft and unauthorized access.

Also: Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now.

The newly introduced remote lock feature is designed to work in tandem with other Microsoft services, such as Intune and BitLocker, to manage a fleet of devices both in-office and remotely across the globe.

It has been revealed that once a device is reported missing or stolen, an admin can disable login access from anywhere without having to fully wipe the laptop or smartphone. Microsoft reports that the lockdown will persist across restarts, even if the device is disconnected from Wi-Fi networks, and can only be lifted by an admin. This means that thieves can’t use your passwords, PINs, or biometric data to circumvent the lock.

While the newly introduced feature allows IT admins to respond quickly when a laptop or phone is reported missing, there are still security gaps that other Windows controls must address. The new lock feature doesn’t erase your data or wipe your device if it can’t be recovered, nor does it isolate the missing device from corporate networks. Therefore, IT admins will still need to access those controls via the Intune and Microsoft Entra dashboards.

Also: You can now restore Windows 11 even if it can’t boot up.

According to recent reports, the remote lock feature also doesn’t change your Microsoft account credentials, so you can use your log-ins on other devices to recover your data, change passwords, and temporarily disable permissions. Finally, Remote lock doesn’t block the device from being booted in Safe Mode, from a USB, in Windows Recovery Mode, or if the storage drive is reimaged; Microsoft highly recommends keeping BitLocker enabled until the device can be wiped or recovered.

Samsung is expected to unveil its Galaxy S27 lineup early next year, and a personal AI assistant might be arriving as well. The so-called Galaxy Claw could perform a variety of functions, including making phone calls, sending text messages and creating appointments, according to Android Authority.

Recent findings suggest that the tech news website discovered Galaxy Claw while digging into Samsung’s Personal Agent Core app, which is a new AI system that connects AI across Samsung apps and Google services. This new system can also pull data from your calendar, Gmail, text messages, delivery info and other sources and also autonomously perform tasks upon your instructions.

Android Authority remarked that coding details for the Personal Agent Core app were shared by The Cipher Project, a Telegram channel that often leaks Samsung software updates, One UI features and unreleased device functions.

A representative for Samsung did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Sources indicate that samsung has had AI functionality on its phones and other devices since January 2024, when the organization introduced Galaxy AI. The main capabilities at that launch included Circle to Search — allowing consumers to search for anything on the screen — as well as live language translation and photo editing.

Over the past two-plus years, Samsung has integrated more AI functionality into its devices, including Google Gemini and Gemini Live. Although Samsung devices have plenty of AI to do things for you, it primarily operates on your command rather than acting as an autonomous agent.

Recent findings suggest that the latest Galaxy Claw system might launch at Samsung Unpacked in January or February, when Samsung could release the Galaxy S27 series, which could include the Ultra flagship. Samsung has not officially revealed what products it will launch at Unpacked.

According to recent reports, according to Android Authority, the Galaxy Claw could connect to various apps on your phone and perform functions for you. Those apps could include Calendar, Contacts, Gallery, Gmail, Messages, Notifications, Perplexity, Phone and Voice Recorder.

It has been revealed that so, in essence, the Claw could create appointments, write and send emails and make phone calls. For example, you could have Claw set up a meeting and send calendar notifications to the attendees with an attached agenda. Or perhaps Claw could call someone for you to tell them where you’re going.

Android Authority remarked other components could be included — Daily Brief, Device Cleaner, Travel Planner and a dedicated widget.

Those tasks would be a major step up from what Galaxy AI can right now do on Samsung phones — live translation, text drafting, photo editing, scam call detection and more.

Adding agentic AI won’t justify the $1,400 or even $1,500 price tag for the S27 Ultra but could help generate customer loyalty, claims tech reviewer Jon Rettinger.

Sources indicate that “People buy the Ultra for the camera, the screen and the S Pen, and that won’t change next year,” Rettinger told CNET. “Where an agent could matter is keeping people. If Galaxy Claw is reading my Gmail, my calendar and my texts and quietly handling the busywork, switching phones gets a lot harder, because I’d be walking away from an assistant that knows how my week runs.”.

Rettinger said Samsung would be wise to include the Galaxy Claw with the upcoming devices and not as a separate subscription service.

According to recent reports, “So, now the pitch is $1,500 for the phone, then a monthly fee for the feature that’s supposed to justify the phone,” Rettinger mentioned. “That’s a tough sell. If Samsung wants this to move hardware, it should come included on the Ultra.”.

In a recent development, people apparently will maintain authority and control over Galaxy Claw, according to Android Authority. The upcoming system would request access to sensitive data such as contacts, photos and calendar events, as well as permission to execute functions such as sending text messages and making calls. The Claw wouldn’t go rogue on you, in other words.

According to recent reports, samsung users might also be able to schedule the Claw to do tasks and functions regularly. Perhaps you need to email or text weekly reminders to someone about something. You could instruct the AI on the task and when to do it each week. It might only require a simple prompt from you, such as, “Please remind my son to take out the garbage by 8 a.m. Monday mornings.”.

It has been revealed that android Authority said tasks could be scheduled by hour, day, weekly and custom intervals. People would also be able to cancel or modify scheduled tasks and check task history.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft has released new information explaining the massive outage that started Thursday morning and affected Microsoft 365, Copilot, and Outlook access in 74 countries, according to Downdetector.
  • According to recent reports, charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform, posted early Monday morning that the outage was due to three factors, including a “latent defect” from a July enhancement to Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers.
  • It has been revealed that “A latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft has released new information explaining the massive outage that started Thursday morning and affected Microsoft 365, Copilot, and Outlook access in 74 countries, according to Downdetector.

According to recent reports, charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform, posted early Monday morning that the outage was due to three factors, including a “latent defect” from a July enhancement to Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers. Low server capacity and peak traffic in the US brought the defect out of hiding, despite no prior reported problems.

It has been revealed that “A latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions. This was due to lock contention inside an internal process which caused the machine to become unavailable,” Lamanna said, noting that the enhancement was deployed safely worldwide without any issues for over three months.

He said Microsoft didn’t find the glitch in testing due to “the different traffic and SKU mix used in our test labs,” because “our load testing tended to focus on our weaker hardware SKUs with fewer cores.”.

Also: Microsoft fixes over 1,000 Windows flaws – and one is being exploited.

Two other factors made matters worse, and left servers useless in less than two hours.

Industry observers note that “A surge in load increased the likelihood for the networking gateways to encounter the contention,” Lamanna noted, explaining that Microsoft 365 maintains two gateway systems. Before the outage started, Teams failed from one to the other, which “changed its traffic patterns.” Simultaneously, he added, “nearly 14% of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service due to an unrelated matter from the previous day.”.

Those two conditions collided and “caused the network gateway to encounter the latent bug from July,” Lamanna concluded. Requests eventually overloaded servers, at which point they stopped responding. At the outage’s low point, over 80% of its servers weren’t responding.

Industry observers note that “When servers lose connectivity, our traffic management systems automatically route users to other healthy endpoints,” Lamanna remarked. “However, the redirected traffic increased the likelihood for the same problem to occur on the remaining endpoints. This caused a cascading failure from server to server as the same amount of load was spread across fewer servers.”.

Also: AI finds zero-day flaws for just $4 now – even mediocre hackers can cash in.

Before Microsoft issued an explanation, some suspected the outage may have been the result of a cyberattack, which both Lamanna and Microsoft’s status account denied.

In a recent development, it’s unclear how many people the outage affected, though Microsoft’s own numbers from January say Microsoft 365 “exceeds 450 million commercial paid seats,” illustrating the scale of the problem. Microsoft deployed an upgrade to fix the outage and gradually applied it to groups of servers. Lamanna said Microsoft would publish a full post-incident review with more details later this week.

Industry observers note that service might be restored, but customers aren’t happy about having lost nearly two full workdays. One think tank told CNN it estimated the outage — which lasted through close of business on Friday for some — resulted in $7 billion in losses, due to many businesses and organizations being unable to access their everyday systems.

Also: If the November Windows update fails to install on your PC, here’s what to do.

The fact that Microsoft’s testing couldn’t find the July issue ahead of time may leave customers wondering when the next dormant defect will strike, and whether the manufacturer is prepared.

Industry observers note that organizations across Europe have been leaving Microsoft in recent years, opting instead for locally-controlled, open-source alternatives. The former CEO of Github launched a decentralized alternative called Entire earlier this year, citing developers’ need for something more reliable, as Github has similarly been plagued with outages.

For many, Teams was barely offline over the two-day period, or was the first service to come back online.

“Several services like Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Office apps failed out of the faulty network gateway infrastructure. That is why those services were restored earlier, with Teams chats and meetings functioning without issue for most of the outage,” Lamanna explained. Other services like Exchange Online can’t fail out.

He added that fixing the outage was slow because waiting traffic hit servers as soon as they came back, rendering them unresponsive just as quickly.

“Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state,” Lamanna said. “Additionally, since the main code defect was a latent bug from several months previous, our normal rollback, flighting, and feature flags were unable to quickly revert the change.”.

On Thursday morning, people began reporting concerns with Outlook, Teams, and Copilot, according to Downdetector. By 1 p.m. ET, the number of reported Outlook outages was nearly 83,000 but had fallen to just under 75,000 by 2:38 p.m. ET. Teams and Copilot reports started dropping significantly by Thursday evening, but many individuals were still reporting issues accessing systems well into Friday morning on X and Reddit. Even Microsoft’s status page was down until around 3 p.m. ET Thursday.

Also: If the November Windows update fails to install on your PC, here’s what to do.

As late as Friday afternoon, the organization didn’t yet have an ETA of when the outage would be fully solved.

Breaking: A Fresh Study Finds Hyperscale Data Centers Emit as Much Carbon as Denmark

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (614 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • During the midterm elections, Americans made one thing very clear: Data centers must be reined in.
  • A vast majority of communities across the country voted to ban or restrict the construction of data centers, as concerns about their impact on the environment and public health grow.
  • A fresh study by Harvard researchers indicates that these fears are not unfounded.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During the midterm elections, Americans made one thing very clear: Data centers must be reined in.

A vast majority of communities across the country voted to ban or restrict the construction of data centers, as concerns about their impact on the environment and public health grow.

A fresh study by Harvard researchers indicates that these fears are not unfounded. The findings published today in Nature Sustainability show that the carbon emissions and energy use of hyperscale data centers amount to as much as those of entire states and more than those of the country of Denmark.

I spoke with Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics and lead author of the paper, to discuss how the team collected data on energy use despite a lack of industry transparency, the rapid evolution of AI infrastructure and future research goals.

Hyperscale data centers are the largest and most powerful data center facilities, featuring thousands of servers to power cloud computing, model training and the global use of AI. Guidi said he was inspired to look into data center emissions and the broader impacts of generative AI after reading a paper on bitcoin mining’s electricity use, which found that just 34 mining facilities, combined, consumed as much electricity as the entire city of Los Angeles.

The study narrowed in on 403 of these facilities to provide the most up-to-date and transparent measures of their electricity use and carbon emissions between May 2024 and April 2025.

Tech companies are not quick to disclose their energy use, so Guidi and his team had to circumvent these obstacles to get accurate metrics. The team used satellite imagery to narrow down 675 candidate sites to 403 verified facilities, estimated annual electricity consumption, and linked them to Environmental Protection Agency data to measure each facility’s carbon emissions.

“I would say the data preparation, data collection and validation were 100% the toughest part of the whole project,” Guidi said during a phone interview, explaining that there is a need for transparency and people should have access to this data.

Industry observers note that during the study, the team found that these hyperscale data centers emitted 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide, more than the entire country of Denmark and far exceeding the last peer-reviewed estimate from 2018. The 403 facilities also used between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours of electricity during the testing period — about 1.8% of all US electricity consumption.

Recent findings suggest that A majority of the electricity (54%) that powers these hyperscale data centers comes from natural gas and coal, despite many tech companies signing corporate pledges to make substantial investments in renewable energy. Fossil fuels have long been known to generate massive amounts of carbon dioxide, exacerbating global warming and climate change, despite many of these tech companies. “We need to distinguish between what companies commit to on paper, and then the actual physical emissions associated with the whole powering of these infrastructures,” Guidi said.

The Harvard team also pointed out that the paper’s data is from last spring, meaning the industry’s 2026 footprint is certainly substantially larger today.

According to recent reports, “I feel like the pace at which the industry is growing is really outpacing the pace at which people like us — scientists — are working in order to understand (HDC) impacts,” Guidi said. “And we’re lagging behind because of the way the system is made.”.

As data centers scale and expand, the research will need to as well, the researchers mentioned. The team is already working to expand its dataset to investigate the broader public health consequences of hyperscale data centers, including water consumption and noise pollution.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Starting this week, customers booking an Uber ride in Las Vegas could be matched with a Zoox autonomous vehicle.

Zoox’s boxy, purpose-built vehicles have been operating for the general public in Sin City for a little over a year via the manufacturer’s own app. But this is the first time Zoox, which is owned by Amazon, is teaming up with a third-party platform like Uber. (You can still hail a ride in Vegas through the Zoox app; the company began charging passengers in August.).

Sources indicate that now, riders who request an UberX, Uber Comfort, Uber Electric, Uber Comfort Electric or Wait & Save could be paired with a Zoox robotaxi, and they won’t have to pay extra. You can boost your chances of being matched with the AV by going to Ride Preferences in the Uber app’s settings. Then tap Autonomous vehicles, and hit the toggle next to Get more autonomous rides.

In a recent development, after you’ve been matched with a Zoox vehicle, you can choose to accept the autonomous ride or opt for a non-AV. Passengers can access 24/7 human support from both the Uber app and inside the Zoox vehicle.

It has been revealed that unlike other autonomous vehicles from companies like Waymo and Wayve, which retrofit cars from third-party manufacturers, Zoox’s purpose-built robotaxis don’t have a steering wheel, driver’s seat or pedals. Instead, there are two rows of seats facing each other, so you can chat more easily with your fellow passengers. The vehicles are bidirectional, making it a little easier to get out of a parking space, for instance. I’ve taken a few Zoox rides in Las Vegas and San Francisco, and despite the robotaxi’s unique design, the experience felt remarkably ordinary, with the vehicle seamlessly navigating through traffic.

Uber and Zoox confirmed their multiyear partnership in March. The companies also plan to hit the road together in Los Angeles in 2027, after Zoox releases there via its own app.

In a recent development, teaming up with Uber could expose Zoox to more customers, since many people already have the ride-hailing app downloaded on their phones. A tourist hub like Las Vegas has become a hotspot for AV companies to test and launch their services, with many people willing to try something new as they get around the city.

“Zoox has built something truly unique, and by bringing its purpose-built robotaxis to Uber, we’re introducing an entirely latest riding experience to more people in Las Vegas, with Los Angeles coming next,” Samarth Kejriwal, global head of autonomous mobility at Uber, said in a statement.

This comes after the dissolution of Uber’s exclusive partnership with Alphabet-owned Waymo in Austin and Atlanta, which Bloomberg reports will end starting early next year. Instead, Waymo reportedly plans to offer rides directly within its own app, as it does in several other locations. Meanwhile, Uber has partnered with dozens of other AV companies, including Aurora, Wayve, Avride, Nuro and May Mobility.

Recent findings suggest that while Waymo is the leader in the self-driving space, Zoox has been ramping up its operations in recent months. Along with Las Vegas, riders can join a waitlist to ride in San Francisco, with aims to roll out its robotaxi service in Miami and Austin. Zoox is also testing its self-driving technology in Seattle, Atlanta, Los Angeles, Dallas, Phoenix, Houston, San Diego and Washington, DC.

    #16012. Industry News: Did a Single Router Ground the Nation’s Flights? Experts Express Doubt

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1059 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cnet ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Did a Single Router Ground the Nation’s Flights? Experts Express Doubt

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1059 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The humble internet router is at the center of another national firestorm.
    • Recent findings suggest that secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy noted Sunday that a single router in Arkansas was to blame for the nearly 5-hour-long ground stop on Friday.
    • FAA investigators zeroed in on a routine network upgrade at a radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, where a copper wire line was being upgraded to fiber optic cable by the contractor L3Harris.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The humble internet router is at the center of another national firestorm.

    Recent findings suggest that secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy noted Sunday that a single router in Arkansas was to blame for the nearly 5-hour-long ground stop on Friday. It was only the second nationwide halt to US air travel since Sept. 11, 2001, leading to the cancellation of 12,462 flights on Friday alone.

    FAA investigators zeroed in on a routine network upgrade at a radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, where a copper wire line was being upgraded to fiber optic cable by the contractor L3Harris. A latest router that came online during the upgrade may have overwhelmed the older equipment, investigators say.

    “Either through contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment, that router that was being replaced as we switched from copper to fiber, it started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system,” Duffy remarked in an interview Sunday.

    In a recent development, this sent a barrage of data through the FAA’s internal communication system — about 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds – that air traffic controllers use to help guide pilots through the country’s airspace. When that new router was turned on, agency officials noticed the same concerns at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, which had undergone similar work weeks before, Duffy stated. The routers at the Arkansas and Texas facilities led to 17 out of the FAA’s 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers experiencing network instability, according to the agency.

    But some aviation experts say this official explanation strains credulity.

    In a recent development, “I don’t think it’s plausible,” Robert W. Mann Jr., the founder of airline analysis and consulting firm R.W. Mann & Tech giant, told CNET. “Given the network architecture, which is fully duplicative and has fallback capabilities on every link and every piece of physical hardware, it’s not credible that one or even two routers would be an issue.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the impacts of the nationwide ground stop are reverberating on the other side of the weekend. As of 3:30 p.m. EST, 333 flights within, into or out of the US have been canceled Monday, according to flight tracking website FlightAware, and more than 3,800 have been delayed.

    The FAA router that grounded tens of thousands of flights looks a lot different from the one that sits in your home. These industrial-grade devices, called switches, are much larger than home Wi-Fi routers and built to withstand harsh conditions. While the agency pointed to the single router in Arkansas as the cause of Friday’s issues, it notes it disabled 60 similar units as a precaution.

    According to recent reports, FAA Administrator Brian Bedford said Saturday that the agency is in the process of replacing around 2,000 Cisco routers with 600 Juniper routers. Could any one of those routine equipment upgrades suddenly overload the FAA’s communications system?

    “What surprised me most is the redundancy part for this type of national infrastructure,” Ilia Rabinovich, vice president at the cybersecurity firm Sygnia, told CNET. “This is one of the first things we discuss with clients in terms of preparedness – having backups, having redundancy connectivity, having different connections that you can migrate to different places.”.

    Mann thought the timing and symptoms pointed to a upcoming $875 million AI-supported air traffic management tool called Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories, or SMART.

    In a recent development, “What they did starting in September at Baltimore-Washington is at a very low level, for about 60 days. It had managed about 180 flights in total over 60 days,” Mann noted. “And then suddenly in November, they confirmed they would implement that system across all 22 continental US air traffic control centers.”.

    “You went from subscale to superscale based upon 60 days of very, very limited testing, and within two days, you had the meltdown that they should have known was likely to occur,” Mann mentioned.

    On Oct. 13, more than 25 lawmakers sent a letter to the FAA asking it to pause the rollout of the tool, citing a lack of transparency and training for air traffic controllers.

    “We have heard from several sources that frontline aviation safety workers were notified of the SMART tool rollout mere days in advance or not at all, giving them no time to learn how the system works, how it is incorporated into their workflow, and what oversight and accountability mechanisms maintain aviation safety standards,” the letter says.

    In a recent development, the FAA states in an FAQ page on the incident that the SMART system wasn’t responsible for the issue. A representative for the agency didn’t immediately respond to CNET’s request for comment.

    The FAA’s acting CTO, Rebecca Guy, said at a press conference Saturday that the FAA identified the routers in Arkansas and Texas and disabled “both of those right away and were able to stabilize our network.” But the Transportation Secretary’s interviews over the weekend didn’t instill a lot of confidence in the FAA network’s resilience.

    Sources indicate that “We have old switches, old routers. We use 1980s little copper lines. It’s an old system that went down and went down everywhere. It got overloaded,” Duffy noted at a Friday night news conference.

    The FAA has upgraded over 3,500 of its communication lines to fiber, but more than 5,000 copper lines are still scheduled to be replaced by the end of 2028. It’s eye-opening to see how reliant the FAA still is on copper lines, a technology that the Federal Communications Commission has for years deemed insufficient for average home internet users.

    Recent findings suggest that it didn’t take long for officials to point to funding as the ultimate cause of Friday’s groundings. Duffy repeatedly called for more funding over the weekend in order to upgrade the outdated system.

    According to recent reports, “The government and FAA are looked on as the piñata here because every time you beat on FAA or beat on the government for not doing a good job, money falls out,” Mann stated. “It didn’t take, what, 6 hours, before we had a cabinet secretary basically saying if we gave him $50 billion, he would fix all this.”.

    Sources indicate that duffy had asked for $30 billion for the FAA in September. After Friday’s fiasco, he increased his request by $20 billion.

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (593 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cnet ↗ Open Full Page

    School Campuses Emerge as the Latest Battleground for Flock Safety Cameras

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (593 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Over the last year, a backlash against surveillance technologies from companies like Flock Safety has caused agencies in communities, including Los Angeles and Dayton, Ohio, to reevaluate or cancel their contracts for tools such as license plate reader cameras and drones.
    • Now, some college and high school campuses are taking the same steps, reconsidering whether the value of identifying potential crime suspects or providing first-responder information is worth the privacy trade-offs.
    • A recent story in The Guardian points to dozens of schools, mostly college campuses, where contracts with Flock have been discontinued or where student protests and activism are pressuring administrations to cut ties.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Over the last year, a backlash against surveillance technologies from companies like Flock Safety has caused agencies in communities, including Los Angeles and Dayton, Ohio, to reevaluate or cancel their contracts for tools such as license plate reader cameras and drones.

    Now, some college and high school campuses are taking the same steps, reconsidering whether the value of identifying potential crime suspects or providing first-responder information is worth the privacy trade-offs.

    A recent story in The Guardian points to dozens of schools, mostly college campuses, where contracts with Flock have been discontinued or where student protests and activism are pressuring administrations to cut ties. Some of the schools that have walked away from Flock include Cornell University, Emory University, Penn State University and Stanford University, where a coalition called Safe Stanford successfully organized to convince school officials. At Stanford, the university chose to switch from Flock to technology from Genetec, which stores data for only an hour and doesn’t share information with third parties.

    Recent findings suggest that some of the most recent campus protests against using Flock technology have been on the University of Iowa campus, where 2,000 petition signatures were delivered to campus police, and at the University of Kentucky, where student groups chanted, “Flock out! Flock off!”.

    Flock, which is one of several companies, including Axon Enterprise, Motorola Solutions and Palantir Technologies, that provide surveillance hardware and software to law enforcement, has been heavily criticized for license plate reader failure rates and abuses within law enforcement.

    In an email to CNET, the Atlanta-based manufacturer declined to offer the number of colleges or schools it works with, though a recent research paper published in Policing & Society put the number at around 150.

    Flock stressed in its email to CNET that customers it contracts with own and control their own data.

    “Students deserve to feel safe at school, and Flock license plate reader technology has a measurable impact on helping to solve crimes and increase public safety,” the spokesperson stated. “Flock LPR cameras capture a point-in-time image of the rear of a vehicle. Flock does not use facial recognition, cannot identify who is inside a vehicle and cannot determine who the vehicle is registered to.”.

    When government agencies like police departments or county sheriff’s offices employ a organization like Flock to provide surveillance services, it typically involves installing cameras in public locations and pointing them at street intersections or on buildings.

    College and high school campuses may have different rules for on-campus surveillance and for public schools. They might also be bound by state laws that also apply to government agencies.

    “Campuses also raise complications ordinary public streets don’t: students often live there, many are minors, and student-privacy laws and school-search rules vary by state, as do limits on how long plate data can be kept and shared,” remarked Amy Peikoff, an attorney for the Pacific Legal Foundation.

    Recent findings suggest that peikoff said that most courts have allowed the collection of the types of data Flock Safety collects. However, Peikoff said that problems can arise regarding how long agencies such as police departments or schools can retain the data they collect. In the past, activists have pointed to abuses that have occurred when law enforcement workers inappropriately accessed or shared information collected by Flock, in some cases, using it for stalking.

    “Maintaining a vast, queryable database of location histories of individuals about whom there’s no particularized suspicion not only presents an opportunity for abuse, but is in itself, I believe, a Fourth Amendment violation,” Peikoff mentioned.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, although the iPhone Duo was released just this fall, Apple is finalizing the foldable’s second generation. According to a Bloomberg report, Apple has already created prototypes for the second iPhone Duo, codenamed V78, and some include a sought-after feature: Face ID.

    Apple reportedly wants to bring Face ID to the foldable, potentially integrating it into the outer display. However, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman notes that Apple appears to be running out of time to finalize its plans for the Duo ahead of a fall 2027 launch.

    Also: iPhone Duo review: Hard to recommend, even harder to put down.

    iPhone launch events typically take place in early September, when Apple releases its new smartphone lineups. To have the iPhones ready for sale on the heels of their announcement, Apple must manufacture the new models well before the launch event.

    Because of this timeline concern, Face ID isn’t guaranteed for the iPhone Duo 2, though it could come to a third generation instead.

    Other planned uogrades — including an Action Button, a telephoto camera, and a thinner, lighter construction — are also noted in the report.

    In a recent development, apple reportedly wants to add an Action Button, the customizable button that performs an action when pressed. The iPhone Duo 2 may combine the Action Button and the Camera Control buttons into a single button, providing a useful physical shortcut instead of adding a new button.

    The report indicates that many customers don’t use the camera control button as often as Apple expected. Combining the camera and action buttons gives Apple the real estate necessary to add both options in an already constrained space.

    Apple also wants to incorporate a telephoto camera into the iPhone Duo, though this is likely to happen in one of the next couple of generations. A telephoto camera would give people greater flexibility to zoom in and capture clear photos of distant objects, which would be an upgrade to the Duo’s photography features.

    Technically, equipping the Duo with a telephoto camera is feasible, but the biggest obstacle is space constraints. A telephoto camera needs more room than a wide-angle one, since it requires additional optical elements to magnify distant objects.

    Apple already uses a tetraprism design in its Pro iPhones, which allows a longer optical path without too much physical depth.

    It has been revealed that apple also wants to reduce the weight and thickness of the iPhone Duo, which is legitimately clunky and cumbersome. To do this, Apple needs to balance the large internal and outer displays, battery capacity, camera array, and the hinge mechanism.

    Also: The iPhone Action Button you’re hardly using has a superpower.

    For many consumers, reducing the weight and thickness of a passport-sized foldable could matter more in buying decisions than adding another button or camera.

    Gurman’s latest report doesn’t mention any planned changes for the iPhone Duo’s hinge mechanism, even after concerns with the first generation’s durability. With manufacturing deadlines fast approaching, however, it’s unlikely that Apple will be able to make changes to the Duo 2 based on consumer feedback. More than likely, these changes would come with the third-generation model.

    CNET tested the iPhone Duo’s hinge mechanism and found that, after around 440,000 cycles, the hinge stopped opening flat on its own. Loosening and other signs of wear were evident after 390,000 folds.

    Also: The best iPhone Duo cases: Expert recommended.

    Given the thinner, lighter construction of a future Duo model, one could assume that changes to the hinge and the foldable’s internal structure are imminent, but this has not been confirmed.

    In a recent development, because Apple will not have enough time to gather feedback on the iPhone Duo before the manufacturing deadlines for the iPhone Duo 2, I don’t expect the second-generation iPhone Duo to be significantly different from its predecessor. We do expect a thinner iPhone Duo 2 and a way to incorporate the Action and Camera buttons.

    #16007. 5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1171 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

    5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1171 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, at the beginning of the year, few organizations were utilizing large language models (LLMs) and AI agents in their cybersecurity workflows, including for discovering and patching vulnerabilities.
    • Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?
    • The capabilities of agentic AI are fast outstripping the speed and scale at which traditional security operations centers (SOCs) can operate.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, at the beginning of the year, few organizations were utilizing large language models (LLMs) and AI agents in their cybersecurity workflows, including for discovering and patching vulnerabilities. According to Google, this is now happening at scale.

    Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

    The capabilities of agentic AI are fast outstripping the speed and scale at which traditional security operations centers (SOCs) can operate. Like it or not, AI has an integral role in the new reality — for the defenders and threat actors.

    Speed and scale are the main reasons enterprises consider adopting AI in SOCs and for security more broadly, and these factors underpin Google’s fresh security forecast for 2027 — Cloud CISO Perspectives. However, without the right precautions, AI security adopters could inadvertently increase their attack surface rather than shrink it.

    With this in mind, these are five ways AI will change the security industry over the next year and what CISOs need to consider going into 2027.

    It has been revealed that alert fatigue is well-known across SOC teams. Alert after alert needs to be trawled through; many are irrelevant or false positives, tying up skilled staff with the mundane, tedious, time-consuming task of triaging them.

    Now that autonomous, AI-driven threats can probe a network, gain entry, and move laterally across it in minutes, chasing threat data and security alerts from multiple systems logged days or weeks ago can’t help a business mitigate them — and certainly not at the speed of the threat.

    Industry observers note that according to Google’s forecast, AI will mean the alert queue quietly disappears. Ramya Chitrakar, VP of engineering at Google Cloud Security, believes that “2027 is the year analysts stop chasing alerts and start shaping outcomes.”.

    Also: AI is both a cyber weapon and a massive target.

    Sources indicate that how? CISOs must change the alert model itself. Instead of human defenders triaging alerts at the start of a cybersecurity incident, the alert becomes final output, with autonomous agents handling “data enrichment, correlation, and triage automatically, surfacing a verified conclusion rather than a raw ticket,” according to Google.

    This means cybersecurity experts can oversee alert handling and verify automated actions, potentially freeing them to focus on other tasks.

    Custom agentic AI is often designed — or at least intended — to work autonomously, with human oversight. However, having thousands of individual agents working across multiple environments can create high-value entry points into corporate networks that cyberattackers target.

    We need to think of agentic AI as more than a tool: each one needs its own identity, like a human employee, to operate within a zero-trust architecture, retain control, and reduce the risk of compromise.

    Also: Your enterprise AI access can be sold for pennies – beware ‘LLM Mixers’.

    In a recent development, however, Heather Adkins, VP of security engineering at Google, thinks this needs to go further and suggests the zero-trust concept shouldn’t stop at the network layer. Instead, Adkins believes it needs to reach the transaction layer.

    According to recent reports, A paper trail for each agent needs to be established, which is impossible to handle manually, and even within a zero-trust framework, AI agents could be given too much scope. Instead, implement verification for each transaction and for every authorization, and assign each AI agent its own least-privilege set of credentials that can be revoked if there is a security incident or the agent is no longer required.

    “When backed by real-time autonomous reasoning, we can dynamically allow a transaction on Tuesday and block the exact same request on Wednesday if conditions look anomalous,” the report notes.

    AI is being used to speed up the development and deployment of new software, and in 2027, security will have to become a continuous system embedded in the software delivery pipeline, according to Google.

    Sources indicate that threat actors have carried out software supply chain attacks over the years, one of the most notable being the SolarWinds incident of 2020. Sandra Joyce, VP of Google Threat Intelligence, states cybercriminals are now poisoning everything from open-source code to software libraries, which AI coding assistants often pull automatically into codebases.

    Also: How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain.

    Sources indicate that bug-fix tickets that take days to respond to and security appearing at the end of a software development cycle no longer work. Instead, writing and securing code must happen simultaneously, with the help of agentic AI, so speed doesn’t compromise security.

    “It’s also crucial that we link live production environments directly back to source code so that defenders can trace a real-world exposure to the exact line of code, validate whether it is genuinely exploitable, and deliver a pre-tested fix at machine speed without breaking production,” Google added.

    As organizations rush to implement AI into their applications and services to appear “AI-first,” innovative, and modern, security may be ignored or treated as an afterthought.

    As a result, we may face a fresh, broader attack surface than we realize, as AI introduces new security challenges, including software vulnerabilities, misconfiguration, bypasses, and indirect prompt injection attacks. Now that AI is also in the hands of all cyberattackers — from script kiddies to state-sponsored groups — auditing corporate networks and infrastructure is crucial.

    It has been revealed that also: Who’s responsible for catching rogue AI agents? You are.

    Penetration testing and red team exercises now need to cover agentic AI. This wasn’t in scope for many red teams only a few years ago, but now that businesses have run with the idea of implementing AI in their workflows, processes, and products, organizations need to identify and fix security challenges introduced by AI before threat actors take advantage of them.

    CISOs should task pen testers with auditing before an autonomous workflow hits production, then combine the results with threat intelligence to ensure defenders have the information they need to bolster network defenses and harden classifiers against fresh and novel attacks.

    The final significant trend we are likely to see in 2027 is tackling agent sprawl to create coordinated teams of AI agents that can rapidly handle security tasks at scale.

    Single AI agents given general instructions won’t cut it when AI-assisted attackers can compromise endpoint devices, enter networks, move laterally, or start stealing data in a far shorter timeframe than before. Instead, CISOs should replace these “generalist” AI agents with specialized, orchestrated teams of AI agents that can meet the demands of defending against AI-driven attacks by employing specialist tooling and skill sets.

    Also: AI agent kill switch urged by Okta-led alliance.

    CISOs also need to ensure that each agent has its own domain training and understanding, memory, and dedicated tools, and can act on its own within set limits, with a central coordinator that knows when to hand a decision to a human. This requires oversight, but in return, organizations will avoid agent sprawl, which the tech giant believes is the next iteration of shadow IT and its associated threats.

    Industry News: CNET Survey: $75 Billion in Holiday Packages Could Be Vulnerable to Lurking Porch Pirates

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, imagine patiently waiting for the special-edition Legend of Zelda Nintendo Switch 2 console or the new iPhone Duo to be delivered to your door — only for it to disappear seconds after arrival.
    • In a recent development, online holiday shopping has become the go-to way for many US adults to conveniently find, compare and buy must-have gifts.
    • CNET’s annual package theft survey polls US adults about their experiences with porch pirates and how they try to prevent it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, imagine patiently waiting for the special-edition Legend of Zelda Nintendo Switch 2 console or the new iPhone Duo to be delivered to your door — only for it to disappear seconds after arrival. That’s the risky reality we’re facing this holiday season because of porch pirates.

    In a recent development, online holiday shopping has become the go-to way for many US adults to conveniently find, compare and buy must-have gifts. But leaving those pricey gifts at your door gives thieves a better chance of snagging them in seconds if you don’t have a plan to store them out of sight.

    CNET’s annual package theft survey polls US adults about their experiences with porch pirates and how they try to prevent it. This year, the average package value is close to $300, and 28% of US adults have had a package stolen, know someone who has or caught an attempted theft within the past year. Yet 20% of US adults don’t use security devices due to hardware costs or monthly subscription fees.

    Sources indicate that but leaving your packages unguarded could be a big risk — especially during the holidays. On the other hand, bad actors have been caught in the act on home security cameras. Is it really enough to deter bad actors, and what more can you do to protect your deliveries?

    In a recent development, CNET’s findings show that some US adults have dealt with porch theft firsthand: 8% had packages meant for themselves or their households stolen within the past year, and 5% had a delivered gift stolen. Very few (1%) caught a theft in the act on a video doorbell or security camera.

    Meanwhile, many US adults know someone who fell victim to package theft — 13% know a neighbor or community member who had a package stolen within the past year, and 12% know someone who doesn’t live in their community who has.

    It has been revealed that “Close to a third of our respondents are personally acquainted with package theft, which is still a high number compared to other problems like break-ins,” said CNET’s senior home security editor, Tyler Lacoma. “Thieves generally look for crimes of opportunity, and few things are easier than a package left on a doorstep, especially if nobody is home.”.

    Surprisingly, most US adults (72%) haven’t experienced package theft or know anyone who has.

    Even though the percentages above may seem low, Lacoma said that package theft typically increases during the holidays when thieves know more deliveries are likely, and newly introduced porch theft tactics are always on the horizon.

    There are reports of thieves trying Wi-Fi jamming to disable live security camera footage while they steal packages. And findings show that some are installing spy cams in high-value neighborhoods to learn your home’s layout and habits to take your packages shortly after they’re delivered. In recent years, pirates have even tracked shipping labels for high-value tech, like iPhones, to steal the package within minutes of arrival.

    According to recent reports, so while the majority of US adults haven’t fallen victim, that shouldn’t be a sign to shrug off the concern or relax your home security measures. Instead, now’s the time to strategy how to safely store your packages if they’re delivered while you’re away.

    It has been revealed that online shopping and deliveries to your door can be a convenient way to check off holiday wish lists, but the average package value this holiday season is less than last year. CNET found that US adults blueprint to have an average of $276.24 in holiday packages delivered during this holiday season. That’s $23.82 less than last year’s average of $300.06.

    By generation, Millennials also have a lower estimated average package value than last year, with an average of $227.25, compared to their 2025 package value of $307.47 — an $80.22 difference, while Gen Z’s package value is only about $7 less than last year. But any package’s value is still worth taking precautions to help prevent it from being stolen.

    According to recent reports, lacoma has thoughts on why that might be. In short, lower spending could mean fewer packages.

    “I wonder if people have also simply gotten fewer packages in general this year due to tariffs, inflation and tech prices. That could pull these numbers down,” stated Lacoma. But there’s a high chance that could be the case considering CNET’s 2026 annual holiday survey, which found that US adult tech spending is down to $808 — which is $123 less than last year’s average of $931.

    Thieves may not always know what’s in boxes they’re stealing but they’re willing to take a chance. We asked US adults which items were stolen in package thefts in the past year to give you a sense of what’s at risk.

    Among the items stolen, apparel and accessories were the most common goods stolen (40%). That’s followed by toys and games (23%). Then there are everyday home basics, like decor, cookware and small appliances (19%).

    But personal tech devices and accessories are still among the items stolen. Small accessories like phone chargers and cases are most common (16%) among tech-related packages stolen. They are followed by audio gadgets like headphones and Bluetooth speakers, along with streaming devices and soundbars (11%, respectively).

    Still, more costly tech like gaming consoles (10%), computers and laptops (9%) and smart home devices (6%) are among devices stolen.

    Recent findings suggest that you shouldn’t leave your packages up to chance. That’s why Lacoma recommends a few safer options to ensure your packages are stored securely after they’re delivered, even beyond keeping an eye on your doorbell or security camera. Instead, keep your packages out of sight with tactics like a delivery box with a code or key or ask for an in-garage delivery.

    “Delivery boxes have reached a new level of popularity in recent years as an effective way to stop porch pirates completely. However, Amazon’s Key service that delivers to your garage is an alternative,” mentioned Lacoma. “Either way, you’ll need to trust delivery people to handle your shipments, unless you want to arrange for pickup at a nearby shipping center, which some people like to combine with other holiday errands.”.

    If you don’t want to install a new security feature, try scheduling your packages to arrive when you know you’re home, requiring a signature from someone you trust or changing your delivery location to a pickup spot, like UPS’ Hold for Pick-Up locations or Amazon Lockers.

    It has been revealed that home surveillance, like outdoor security cameras and video doorbells, can deter package thieves who don’t want to risk getting caught on camera. But US adults have mixed feelings about their effectiveness in protecting against package theft.

    It has been revealed that there are two deterrents that are keeping US adults from having security devices — cost and privacy. Findings show that 20% of US adults lack home security measures due to hardware costs or monthly subscription fees. That’s followed by 9% who don’t want to use cameras because of privacy concerns.

    In a recent development, “Fortunately, the right home security picks can solve both these problems,” stated Lacoma. “Brands like Tapo, Eufy, Aqara and even Google Nest offer package detection and alerts for free, so you don’t have to worry about extra fees.”.

    Lacoma added that many companies also offer ways to use local video storage and local AI detection so nothing is stored in the cloud. There are also features, such as customizable privacy zones, to minimize privacy concerns when used with the right precautions.

    In a recent development, among all US adults, only 14% have security devices with a monthly subscription that lets them save or playback video. By comparison, 12% have security devices but no subscription.

    Those percentages could be low for a few reasons, including the overall perception of how helpful surveillance and security really are against porch theft. Eleven percent of US adults don’t think security devices deter porch thefts. It’s a valid concern since 4% fell victim to package theft or an attempted theft despite having security devices. And some US adults (9%) use security devices to get proof of a theft after the fact — not to prevent it.

    Recent findings suggest that but that doesn’t mean you should ignore the possibility of package theft — especially during the holidays. Even if you don’t want to install cameras or new security devices, make a plan to protect your packages and avoid the headache of package theft over the holidays.

    In a recent development, “Remember, the simple presence of a security camera is enough to make many thieves look elsewhere – interviews have confirmed it,” noted Lacoma. “And with today’s phone alerts about package detection, you can usually check on a package only seconds after it appears, or bring up footage if it unexpectedly vanishes, letting you take action fast. Upcoming practices like delivery boxes or in-garage delivery help address risks in concrete ways, too.”.

    CNET commissioned YouGov Plc to conduct the survey. All figures, unless otherwise stated, are from YouGov Plc. The total sample size was 2,016 adults. Fieldwork was undertaken between Oct. 23–27, 2026. The survey was carried out online. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all US adults (aged 18 plus).

    The $75 billion figure was calculated by multiplying the average value of deliveries each US adult expects to receive by the 2025 US population of adults ages 18 and over calculated by the US Census Bureau.

    Oura Ring Adds a Jet Lag Feature for Time Zone Travelers

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (507 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that traveling to newly introduced places is good for the soul, but then there’s jet lag, which can cause fatigue, headaches, insomnia and even nausea during your trip.
    • A press release explained that Jet Lag Plan was developed using a March 2025 study conducted by the National University of Singapore.
    • Jet Lag Plan is specifically designed for customers who travel across at least three time zones and is based on typical sleep patterns, flight itinerary and chronotype.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that traveling to newly introduced places is good for the soul, but then there’s jet lag, which can cause fatigue, headaches, insomnia and even nausea during your trip. Oura, maker of the Oura Ring, wants to help you combat these effects with its latest feature, Jet Lag Plan, which debuted on Tuesday.

    A press release explained that Jet Lag Plan was developed using a March 2025 study conducted by the National University of Singapore. The study analyzed de-identified data covering 1.5 million nights of sleep from over 57,000 Oura members to determine how sleep shifted before and after about 65,000 long-distance trips.

    Jet Lag Plan is specifically designed for customers who travel across at least three time zones and is based on typical sleep patterns, flight itinerary and chronotype. The latter describes whether you’re a morning person, a night person or somewhere in between.

    Oura uses 40 to 90 days of sleep timing and activity and average body temperature trends to assign customers one of six chronotypes: early morning type, morning type, late morning type, early evening type, evening type and late evening type. This can change over time.

    In a recent development, both your chronotype and sleep history also inform your circadian low point. Usually around 4 a.m., this is when your body temperature is at its lowest and you’re the most ready for sleep.

    In the Oura app, you can start a Jet Lag Plan in one of four ways: by adding travel from the Today tab, selecting “Jet Lag” from the app menu, asking the AI-powered Oura Advisor to create a plan for your upcoming trip or responding to a prompt when Oura detects that your phone has changed time zones.

    In addition to your flight details, you’ll also want to share the reason for your trip, as a work-related Jet Lag Plan will differ from a vacation one.

    Your Jet Lag Proposal will then populate with a recommended schedule for sleep, caffeine, activity and light exposure before, during and after your trip, with reminders and the ability to mark actions as complete. You can request adjustments to this plan using Oura Advisor.

    During your trip, you’ll be able to compare your readiness score to the typical score for similar trips. This is based on data from 10 million trips already taken by Oura members.

    Once your trip ends, you’ll receive a report comparing your sleep and readiness scores before and during your trip.

    Jet Lag Blueprint is now available to Oura members whose language is set to English. It works with an Oura Ring 3 or newer on both Android and iOS.

    The latest Oura Ring 5 starts at $399, while a membership is $6 per month or $70 per year.

    Industry observers note that although earnings season -- the six-week period when most S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.04%) companies report their quarterly operating results -- garners most of the glory on Wall Street, Form 13F filing season can be just as valuable. A 13F allows investors to track which stocks Wall Street's savviest money managers bought and sold in the latest quarter.

    Billionaire Stanley Druckenmiller of Duquesne Family Office is an asset manager with a lengthy track record of outperforming Wall Street's benchmark stock indexes. According to Duquesne's newest 13F, he sent shares of Google parent Alphabet (GOOGL -0.54%)(GOOG -0.53%) to the chopping block in the third quarter, while at the same time piling into Elon Musk's Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +1.78%), better known as SpaceX.

    Duquesne Family Office's billionaire boss has been a busy bee. Image source: Getty Images.

    Duquesne Family Office's 13F shows that Druckenmiller sold all 336,300 Class A (GOOGL) Alphabet shares, worth more than $120 million as of June 30, during the September-ended quarter.

    Profit-taking is the most logical explanation for this selling, but it may not be the only one.

    For instance, Druckenmiller is an active trader. The average top-20 holding in Duquesne's investment portfolio has been held for less than seven months. This indicates that its billionaire boss isn't afraid to ring the register when the opportunity presents itself.

    NASDAQ · As of 9:55 AM ET 11/17/26.

    But historical precedent and valuation may have also played a role in Stanley Druckenmiller's decision to dump his fund's entire position in Alphabet.

    In a May 2024 interview with CNBC, he claimed, "Artificial intelligence (AI) might be a little overhyped now, but underhyped long term." Having invested over several decades, Druckenmiller likely recognizes that every major tech innovation has needed time to mature.

    In a recent development, furthermore, Alphabet's otherworldly spending on the AI infrastructure build-out resulted in the tech giant reporting negative free cash flow (FCF) for the September-ended quarter. Though Alphabet still possesses a rock-solid moat in internet search and is delivering jaw-dropping sales growth from Google Cloud, a short-term shift to negative FCF may have left Druckenmiller skittish about the company's near-term prospects.

    At the other end of the spectrum, Duquesne's billionaire chief scooped up 202,125 shares of SpaceX, worth over $30 million at the end of September.

    The lure of SpaceX is its leadership as a space infrastructure and AI hyperscaling giant. The company's prospectus pointed to a $28.5 trillion addressable market, $26.5 trillion of which traces back to its AI services. SpaceX has lined up several graphics processing unit-leasing deals, indicating there's substantial demand for its services.

    While SpaceX broke records with its initial public offering, it's anything but a safe or surefire investment.

    For example, SpaceX's corporate bond prices have been sinking almost precipitously since their issuance in June. Bond prices sink when traders become worried about a company's ability to repay its debt obligations. Musk's company has yet to demonstrate that its operating model is time-tested.

    Industry observers note that great look at the SpaceX shares unlock schedule as well as the potential passive buying schedule from @JSeyff @FrancisSharoon Depending on the early post-IPO returns, this could really play with and disperse the returns of "passive" funds (which is why there's arguably no such thing as passive). $SPCX.

    Furthermore, SpaceX arguably represents the greatest fleecing of retail investors in Wall Street's storied history. Rather than employing the typical 180-calendar-day lockup period for insiders, Musk's company is using a staggered and accelerated lockup schedule that allows some high-ranking executives and early investors to cash out well before the 180-day mark.

    It's hard to argue with Druckenmiller's track record of outperformance, but SpaceX is rife with red flags.

    • “Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, remarked in the press release.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that apple is exploring how people use AI for their health, presumably to build its own AI health coach. On Sunday, it launched the Apple Health AI Usage Study, which could contribute to the next AI health experience Apple builds by measuring the quality of AI health responses, comprehension, and everyday health behaviors, according to a press release.

    According to recent reports, apple is conducting the study in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform widely used by healthcare professionals. The study examines the relationship between conversational AI tools, like chatbots, and the people who use them.

    “Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, remarked in the press release.

    Also: Apple Watch Series 12 review: Finally, the health tracker I’ve been waiting for.

    In a recent development, participants are encouraged to share their HealthKit data and query the health app with questions. The study will also explore how AI tools can best prepare patients ahead of clinical visits. Apple will monitor the AI’s clarity and approachability when providing medical information, and each response or recommendation will be linked to peer-reviewed clinical citations. Responses could be unclear or incomplete, which is why Apple is rolling this out as a study to explore a responsibly designed AI health assistant.

    Apple often launches studies for features it would like to develop in the future. For example, many of the hearing health features launched on the AirPods were a direct result of the findings from Apple’s Hearing Study.

    Also: Athenahealth patients can ask Claude about their medical records now.

    The AI usage study comes on the heels of the revamped Health app’s debut, which launches officially next month. It also arrives amid a bevy of AI health coaches, popping up alongside companion health devices. Google debuted its AI Health Coach in Google Health Premium last year, and Oura launched a proprietary AI model for women trained on medical standards and research from Oura’s in-house team of board-certified clinicians.

    According to recent reports, A growing number of Americans are relying on AI for medical advice. A recent survey from Pew Research Center found that 34% of US adults have talked with a chatbot for medical advice. As AI proliferates, that percentage will only increase.

    “Patients and clinicians are both turning to AI, but the tools they use are being built and tested in separate worlds,” said Robert M. Wachter, M.D., UCSF’s professor and chair of the Department of Medicine, in the press release.

    Apple and other tech companies are building for this latest health normal, and the AI usage study indicates that Apple isn’t taking the responsibility lightly.

    In a recent development, if you’re interested in participating in Apple’s study, it’s open to 200,000 eligible participants age 21 and older in the US. You’ll need a phone with Apple Intelligence enabled (the iPhone 15 Pro or later), running iOS 26 or later. You can download the study app to learn more and enroll.
