    Hit by the FAA Ground Stop? How to Get Your Money Back

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1373 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, an estimated 1.5 million travelers had their flight intends upended on Friday, Nov.
    • Recent findings suggest that that ground stop lifted at 8:15 p.m.
    • In a recent development, nerdWallet travel writer Craig Joseph was among those affected.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, an estimated 1.5 million travelers had their flight intends upended on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, after the Federal Aviation Administration unveiled a rare nationwide ground stop. That number comes from the flight data firm Cirium, which tracked passengers scheduled to depart U.S. airports that day after the stop was declared. The ground stop lasted more than four hours.

    Recent findings suggest that that ground stop lifted at 8:15 p.m. ET on Friday, but the ripple effects could be massive. Planes are out of position for the weekend, and some travelers are still trying to reach their destinations or get refunds on flights and other expenses.

    In a recent development, nerdWallet travel writer Craig Joseph was among those affected. He was flying out of Asheville, North Carolina, for a one-night trip to a college football game, and learned his flight was delayed by three hours. Because it was a quick trip, and he had booked with frequent flyer miles that could be redeposited into his account, he canceled. Moments later, his flight — and every other one on the departures board — was canceled.

    He canceled his hotel before the deadline, too, so his only sunk cost was the football ticket. But not all travelers will be so lucky.

    If your travel looks were impacted, here's how you can get your money back.

    Industry observers note that don’t count on calling customer service. Major airlines have been overwhelmed with customers asking for help.

    As of Friday night, Southwest’s automated phone number remarked it would take several hours to get a callback from a human. American Airlines’ automated line said it would take at least two hours to reach a human. Frontier Airlines wouldn’t even let us speak to a human, and instead sent us to a chatbot.

    In a recent development, skip the chatbots and long waits. Instead, do this:.

    Check the airline’s app or website, and look for any emails or other alerts. Most airlines are proactively notifying affected passengers with rebooking options, and you may be automatically rebooked.

    Get a refund or rebook online or through the airline's app. Every major airline has issued a travel waiver due to the ground stop, which gives you more flexibility to rebook without a change fee, often without charging for fare differences. More on that below.

    Check your travel insurance. Because the ground stop was outside the airlines' control, they may not offer vouchers for hotels or food. If you paid these costs out of pocket, you might be able to get reimbursed from your travel insurance policy, if you purchased one, or your card's coverage. More on that below, too.

    Under U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) rules, you are entitled to a full refund if your flight is canceled or significantly delayed — no matter the reason — and you decide not to travel and turn down other forms of compensation like travel credits. The money must be delivered to your original payment method, even if you bought nonrefundable tickets.

    If your flight disruption meets the DOT criteria, make sure you're getting a full refund. Some airline waivers offer a travel credit as a default option. Credits typically expire, and you won't get value from them until you redeem them. With a refund, you can get your money back within days.

    If you booked with points or miles, you'll generally get those redeposited to your loyalty account, plus a refund of any taxes and fees you paid.

    In a recent development, but if you still want to forge on with your travels, most airlines are allowing affected passengers to rebook new flights without owing a change fee or fare difference, which is more generous than usual. If your original travel dates were Nov. 13 or 14, and you purchased your tickets on or before Nov. 12 or 13, you're likely eligible for these flexible change policies.

    Depending on the airline, you might have even more flexibility. For example, Southwest’s more generous rebooking policy applies to flights scheduled through Monday, Nov. 16.

    Sources indicate that just note that each airline has its own limitations on when you must take that newly introduced flight, so check with your airline to ensure you book within the allowed window. Here are the waiver pages for major airlines:.

    Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines.

    Right now, you and everyone else who was supposed to be on that Friday afternoon flight are vying for limited seats on aircraft flying the same route over the next few days. Get creative if the flight you need is booked up. Think about whether a nearby airport might be possible. You might also opt for a train or rental car.

    If your flight disruption also cost you a hotel night, a rental car, a concert or sports ticket, or some other prepaid piece of your trip, here's your best chance at getting that money back, too:.

    Call the hotel or rental property directly. Although not guaranteed, your host may waive a cancellation penalty or no-show fee for a documented flight disruption like this one. Have your canceled or delayed flight confirmation handy, and ask kindly.

    Sources indicate that for nonrefundable event tickets like concerts or sports games, you’re unlikely to get a direct refund. Check the specific event's refund policy first (and it never hurts to ask!), but your best bet in most cases is reselling the ticket through a platform like StubHub, SeatGeek or Vivid Seats rather than counting on a refund from the original seller.

    Keep every receipt and email confirmation. Whether you're asking a hotel for an exception or filing an insurance claim, having your original flight confirmation, the cancellation or delay notice and your other prepaid reservations documented in one place will make every one of these conversations faster.

    If you have a standalone travel insurance policy: Travel delay and missed connection benefits may cover you for a disruption like this one, according to the insurance marketplace Squaremouth. If you already hold a policy, contact your provider's 24-hour emergency assistance line directly rather than waiting to file a claim after the fact.

    If you don't think you bought travel insurance, check your card terms. Many premium travel credit cards include travel insurance for covered events as a card benefit, assuming you paid for the trip with your card. But in this case, trip cancellation and interruption coverage likely wouldn't apply, because covered events are limited to things like illness, injury and inclement weather.

    Recent findings suggest that but trip delay coverage (which typically applies after a delay of 6 to 12 hours) often covers "equipment failure," so it's more likely to apply here — if the ground stop is deemed to be an equipment failure. This coverage would reimburse "reasonable" expenses during a delay, like meals and lodging. Save your receipts so you're ready to file a claim, but keep in mind that card terms vary and the claim might be denied.

    The backlog from Friday's ground stop is expected to keep disrupting flights through the weekend. If you have a flight in the coming days, recheck your specific flight status before heading to the airport even if things looked fine an hour ago.

    And whatever you were counting on — a refund, a rebooking or an insurance payout — make sure you move fast, document everything and don't assume you only have one option. With airline waivers, DOT refund rules and travel insurance, you might have more ways to get your money back than you think.

    As for Joseph, he’s still trying to resell his football ticket.

    Recent findings suggest that nov. 15, 2026: This article has been updated to clarify how credit card travel insurance benefits might apply here.

    #16001. Google’s Xreal Aura, Reviewed: The Weird Evolution of VR Into Glasses Is Already Underway

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3276 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cnet ↗ Open Full Page

    Google’s Xreal Aura, Reviewed: The Weird Evolution of VR Into Glasses Is Already Underway

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3276 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Let me tell you about a strange, fascinating and rough tweener product called Xreal Aura.
    • It has been revealed that there are VR headsets, and there are smart glasses.
    • The Xreal Aura shoots for the moon, aiming to bridge glasses and VR, and to shrink everything down on the go.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Let me tell you about a strange, fascinating and rough tweener product called Xreal Aura.

    It has been revealed that there are VR headsets, and there are smart glasses. And there’s a newly introduced class of devices that’s falling right in between. What do we call these things? I have no idea. The category includes the Meta VR Glasses coming next year and now the Aura, a collaboration by Google and Xreal.

    The Xreal Aura shoots for the moon, aiming to bridge glasses and VR, and to shrink everything down on the go. It’s often fascinating, and more often frustrating. At times, it almost feels like a VR headset. At other times it feels like a superpowered version of the tethered display glasses that Xreal and several others already make, that act like wearable monitors for your phone or laptop or almost anything else.

    I think it’s actually an experimental bridge to a future where phones will play nicer with advanced smart glasses. Those future glasses could create floating displays and workspaces all around you, if you wish. Consider the Aura, in a way, Google’s early attempt to get there.

    Recent findings suggest that emphasis on early. Right now, the Xreal Aura’s features, OS and especially inputs feel rough to use at times and sometimes hard to get into a natural flow with. But it shows what something of this size could be capable of with more software and input-flow tweaks. And when it does work, it feels wildly like a portable VR/AR headset in a way I’ve never really seen before.

    According to recent reports, the Aura aspires to be a shrunk-down version of last year’s Samsung Galaxy XR, an expensive mixed-reality headset similar to Apple’s Vision Pro. Like the Galaxy XR, the Aura runs Android XR, a variant of Android that floats apps all around. It even runs VR apps. At times it gets close. Other times, it’s not nearly close enough.

    What’s wild about the Aura is that it folds down into a case that’s truly small enough to slide into my bag. But setting up and using the Aura often involves patience and experimentation. When it works, it’s a heck of a peek at a future that’s likely around the corner. But the hoops you have to jump through to make it happen sometimes make me want to hop out.

    Sources indicate that android XR is Google’s OS for AR/VR/AI devices and wearables, and aims to connect glasses and headsets of all shapes and sizes to Google and Gemini services and apps. The Samsung Galaxy XR, released last year, was the first. Coming up next, in just a few weeks, are Google and Samsung’s Warby Parker- and Gentle Monster-designed AI smart glasses.

    It has been revealed that the Xreal Aura is more Galaxy XR than smart glasses, in concept: It’s an AR/VR headset that you can take on the go. The glasses connect with a USB-C cable to an included processor puck that runs Android XR. It can display Android apps in both 2D and immersive 3D.

    In a recent development, the Aura supports hand tracking and can allow full spatial movement to place floating 3D objects or play immersive games. It can float apps all around you, and you can navigate apps at the same time. You can use hand tracking to open or tap those apps, or a trackpad that’s built into the top of the processor puck. You can also pair a Bluetooth keyboard, or game controller, or a mouse, like I’m doing.

    The kit tucks into an included carry case that’s smaller than the one I carry my Nintendo Switch 2 in. It’s easy to pack away for travel. I love this part of the Aura so, so much.

    It’s $1,279 for the version with 256GB of storage and 12GB RAM or $1,499 for 512GB/16GB, but it’s on sale until the end of the year for $1,099/$1,299. That onboard storage is all you get, though. There’s no expandable microSD card slot. I reviewed the 256GB version.

    The display tech in the Aura is an enhanced version of what’s already on Xreal’s other tethered display glasses, and similar to what Viture and TCL RayNeo use. The twin micro OLED displays are impressively bright and crisp, projected via prisms to look like they’re floating in the room with you. The “birdbath” display tech means the lenses are chunky and odd-looking, but they’re also a lot bigger and better-looking than what’s possible on display-enabled wireless glasses like Meta’s Ray-Ban Displays.

    In a recent development, they have a 70-degree field of view, something that beats out previous generations of AR glasses like Magic Leap or the upcoming Snap Specs. The fidelity, although capping at 1,920×1,200 pixels per eye, is also really crisp and great for movie watching or games (up to 120Hz refresh). It’s enough to feel like a massive movie screen is projected across the room or to lay out a virtual computer monitor, but there are clear edges where the image is still cut off compared to VR headsets (which tend to have 90 degree or better fields of view).

    When running VR apps, which this can shockingly do, the graphics look sharp but narrowly framed. It’s good enough to use VR in a pinch, though: I floated through 3D Immersive Google Maps, dragging and scrolling with my fingers in the air, or played the VR role-playing game Demeo, exploring a tabletop board game dungeon, or played back 360-degree videos on YouTube. But the limits of the viewing field become a lot more stark in these modes, making me wish I had a VR headset instead. Then again, I never travel with VR headsets, and I’d travel with this.

    It has been revealed that the display’s visuals seemed to tear a few times while playing YouTube videos. Tracking, using the built-in cameras, also sometimes drifted. Mostly, the displays stayed where I put them, but sometimes they’d shift slightly out of alignment.

    The processor puck means the Xreal Aura can open up most Android and Chrome-based apps I can think of, but not all of them. The Qualcommm Snapdragon Reality Elite chip on the puck seems more than zippy enough to handle whatever multiple games and apps (even VR ones) I throw at it, but not all Android apps are available: Developers can choose not to opt in, as with Netflix and Disney Plus, but they can be loaded up in-browser.

    It has been revealed that other apps aren’t necessarily optimized for the fluid way the Aura can open an app in any size. I watched a Jets game on Paramount Plus on the Aura, and it stayed in a fixed window size. I could move closer or further away, but it wouldn’t enlarge.

    The whole Aura interface feels fresh-ish, even if you’ve used VR. The glasses enable hand tracking that’s surprisingly OK: Tapping and pinching works, and an extended pointer can reach at a distance and click and drag or adjust windows. When my hand passes in front of the Aura’s display, it even gets overlaid with a virtual hand mapped onto mine, like VR.

    There’s no eye tracking, though, something Apple Vision Pro, Samsung Galaxy XR and Meta VR Glasses do. Eye tracking is helpful: It means you can lock into something and click it without lifting your hand. Here, I found I had to lift and aim my hand a lot, like an interactive remote. Hand tracking does work somewhat below the display’s field of view, but you often won’t know if you’re interacting until that hand’s lifted up higher. This is where the Aura’s smaller-than-VR viewing area becomes a problem.

    It has been revealed that it’s particularly an issue when playing some VR games. I tried Synth Riders, a popular fitness music movement game that’s also on Android XR. I could see what was further off in front of me, but the limited viewing area meant my hands were out of sight when in my peripheral vision, so I couldn’t reach for targets near me or off to the sides.

    There’s a second way to control Aura: The processor puck itself has a touchpad across its whole top. Hold it and it’s a touch remote: I can drag my finger and touch-click. On a table next to a paired keyboard, it’s a trackpad.

    That’s super clever, but the trackpad’s performance ranged from OK to poor depending on the apps I ran. There are some multitouch elements too, but it still felt less effective as a headset control than I wanted.

    The puck has discrete volume controls and a power button with a fingerprint sensor for secure logins. But the side button wasn’t always in an easy place to press, depending on how I held the puck.

    You could also just use voice to control things: Saying “Hey Google” or launching live Gemini can open apps, handle dictation and feel like a control system of sorts. But Gemini can’t always do things in apps. It’s more of a launcher.

    There aren’t a ton of unique immersive Android XR experiences, unfortunately, even a year after the Samsung Galaxy XR debuted. The Aura can technically run almost all of those same apps, including many 2D ones that show up on the Google Play store in-headset. On the plus side, VR apps working at all on glasses this small feels like magic, despite some limits.

    According to recent reports, demeo, one of several VR games I found that run on these glasses, looks great and is surprisingly playable. I can cast up a virtual tabletop RPG game in front of me, and my hands bring up cards that I can pick and play on the field. An included Galapagos immersive 3D documentary app looks lovely.

    YouTube and Google Maps are once again stars of Android XR, just like they were on Galaxy XR when I reviewed it last year. YouTube has plenty of 3D and 360-degree videos you can view, and Google Maps’ immersive 3D earth modes and, occasionally, 3D scanned interior locations are still great to browse on the Aura’s smaller screens.

    Sources indicate that I fell in love with a demo of Sock Puppet Superstar, too. It’s a hand-puppet-singing VR game that works well on the Aura.

    Mixed reality VR experiences that try to project a few simple things into a room work best, effectively turning the glasses into augmented reality. Cubism, a hand-tracking enabled puzzle game I’ve played on other VR headsets, works well here too. The accuracy of the hand tracking isn’t always great for precision gripping the corners of the virtual floating blocks, though.

    Sources indicate that the refresh rate on these VR apps isn’t as ultrasmooth as on Quest 3 or Steam Frame, but they do look sharp. Except, as I stated before, the viewing area ends up clipped more narrowly, so immersion feels blindered.

    Some VR apps didn’t run at all, though. A VR air hockey game on Android XR wouldn’t let me use my hands to control the pucks, for some reason. I know this is a prelaunch review of the Aura, but expect some apps to act oddly. You can sideload APKs of other VR apps, which is great. Google’s AI Studio tools also work in spatial 3D in these glasses, which means you could vibecode experiences on them.

    Think of the Aura as a pair of super-powered Xreal glasses with a better viewing area and an included processor puck. Xreal’s existing line of other display glasses float microOLED displays via a USB-C tether in a similar way. The Aura glasses have similar Xreal controls on the arm, but they’re modified to Android XR interface controls that are a little different. There are volume buttons, a button that changes the dimming level of the electrochromic lenses from clear to nearly full black, and a top button that brings up the home app grid when clicked once, or introduces live Gemini when held.

    Industry observers note that there’s also an array of three built-in cameras that handle room tracking, visual awareness for Gemini and hand tracking. Two are in the corners of the frame, one’s above the nose. Xreal’s other glasses, for the most part, are camera-free unless you buy a snap-in module.

    The prism-like lenses that reflect the microOLED displays from the top of the frame are flatter like the Xreal One Pro line, and prescription lens inserts snap in the same way – I used the ones from the Pro and they work fine.

    It has been revealed that speakers are embedded in the arms, pumping out audio that sounds as good as Xreal’s other glasses. Fine for games and movies, but you might prefer earbuds for isolation and privacy.

    Sources indicate that the display’s field of view, at 70 degrees, is bigger than Xreal’s largest size on the One Pro (57 degrees), and it feels like a larger projected display in front of me. The resolution is still just the same as Xreal’s other recent glasses, but things still look crisp, even for reading.

    It has been revealed that sizewise, they’re like many other tethered glasses: bulkier and weirder than normal glasses, but a lot lighter than any VR headset. Three sets of nosepads are included for fit adjustment, and the arms bend at several angles, too.

    I’m writing this review now in the Aura, at my dining room table, with a separately sold folding wireless keyboard made by Xreal. The keyboard performance in Chrome and Docs is fantastic. The trackpad, not quite as much. But I really feel like I can write on this.

    Navigating Chrome and work apps also is possible: Logged into my office’s Google-based system, I’ve been handling emails and chats and little needs fine.

    In a recent development, getting files on and off the Aura is the trick. I’m Mac- and iPhone-based, so I’d need to put things in Drive and Google apps to triangulate more easily.

    In a recent development, but what’s also impressive is that I can plug in other devices, including my MacBook, and use the Aura as a virtual screen. I can float my MacBook and the Aura apps side by side.

    Here’s the catch: My MacBook keyboard only controls my Mac, and the Aura’s keyboard and hand tracking only work for the Aura apps. So I need two keyboards side by side to multitask.

    To be clear, no one’s handled handing off of peripherals between connected devices well, not even Apple. But it points to the biggest thorn in Aura’s device-bridging dreams.

    According to recent reports, connecting to lots of other devices via the Xreal Aura is a wild experience. You just need to cable in with a DisplayPort-ready USB-C cable to do it. The second cable included in the Aura box won’t do it; oddly, that’s just a charging cable.

    Right now, I’m connecting the fresh iPad Mini and casting a second display up in the air. I’m typing on a Logitech keyboard and mouse paired to the iPad, because the Xreal inputs won’t control it. But the point, mainly, is that it connects. And Gemini can still give me feedback on what it sees on my iPad’s virtual screen.

    Recent findings suggest that whatever you plug in can cast a virtual monitor in-glasses: MacBook, iPhone, Steam Deck. Shockingly, even a Nintendo Switch 2 works, something Xreal’s team has been excited about. There are caveats: The Switch 2 goes into docked mode and needs the Joy-Cons detached, and only certain higher-fidelity DisplayPort USB-C cables work. I played Ocarina of Time on the Aura’s screen and it looked great, but the framerate was a bit lower than what I get on the Switch 2 normally. But again, I can ask Gemini questions about the game as I’m playing, and it sees and gives me answers, provided I’ve clicked a little on-screen toggle to share my screen with Gemini’s visual mode.

    Bridging between devices is exciting to me, but it’s really just limited to treating the input like a video-in that pops on a second screen in-glasses. Meta’s VR Glasses will do this too. It’s a great bonus addition, but having to cable both my glasses and my other device to the Aura puck means too many cables for my comfort.

    Sources indicate that the glasses also work on their own without the puck, defaulting to standard Xreal glasses firmware and controls. That’s great if I want to use them with my laptop/phone/etc on the fly without needing the Aura puck, at least.

    Turning on Gemini Live with a press of the top button on Aura’s glasses means you can have Gemini in your life constantly, if you wish. Toggle a little upward-arrow icon to share your camera feed and on-screen apps, and suddenly Gemini can also describe YouTube videos for you, or read what you’re writing, or tell you what’s in your hand.

    Industry observers note that it’s an all-seeing assistant that can even work with Google’s circle-to-search, although that feature’s hard to trigger (press and hold my fingers and click to bring it up, it seems). But I can then circle something in front of me, capture it, and Google AI search brings up results instantly (a book I’m holding, a freezeframe on TV or something on one of my virtual screens).

    This is a step beyond the type of live, camera-enabled AI modes in smart glasses. It can see the world via its cameras and all the virtual apps that get conjured.

    That being said, it’s hit or miss. The video feed quality isn’t great, so the AI can’t always read things at a distance. But I wore the Xreal Aura across my kitchen, making coffee while floating a YouTube window in front of me and talking to Gemini, and it felt like some sort of cyberpunk future I’d only experienced in bits and pieces before. It’s something you could walk around with, technically, but not a device I’d wear all day (nor is it designed to be).

    It has been revealed that xreal promises four hours of battery life on the Aura, which is more than most VR headset claims of 2 to 3 hours. In practice, it feels good. I can use it for several hours and still have a fair amount of battery left, which seems promising. I’ve only been testing for a week, though.

    Recent findings suggest that but the processor puck can overheat. The puck has venting fans that can pump very warm air, and it’s not meant to be put in a pocket, even though that’s exactly what I want to do with it when I’m wearing Aura on my face. Instead, there’s an included belt clip. I tried putting it in my pocket, and pretty soon I got an overheating warning pop-up message. Don’t put it in your pocket.

    Recent findings suggest that I don’t think I’ve ever been as fascinated and borderline overwhelmed as I have with the Xreal Aura. It points in all sorts of directions for where phones, AI assistants and glasses can be heading. Could this little tweener device be my portable workstation eventually?

    Right now it’s more of an experiment with fascinating side benefits. It can’t replace a standard VR headset, though parts come close.

    The Xreal Aura tested even my latest-device tolerance, although I see amazing glimmers. It’s coming with me on my next trips for sure, and I’ll let you know what happens when I do. But it’s not yet the true fusion solution I’m waiting for. And yet, I’m still convinced that the concept, remixed and refined, will be.

    CME vs. Toast: Which Financial Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1019 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Investors often weigh the stability of established financial giants against the high-growth potential of modern software platforms.
    • Industry observers note that CME Group operates a global exchange for futures and options, serving as a critical piece of market infrastructure.
    • CME Group operates the world's most diverse derivatives marketplace, offering trading for asset classes ranging from equities to energy and agriculture.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Investors often weigh the stability of established financial giants against the high-growth potential of modern software platforms. Choosing between CME Group (CME -1.03%) and Toast (TOST -1.46%) requires balancing the two paths.

    Industry observers note that CME Group operates a global exchange for futures and options, serving as a critical piece of market infrastructure. Toast provides the digital backbone for restaurants, handling everything from payments to point-of-sale hardware. Both companies play essential roles in the financial stocks landscape but face distinct growth drivers as we look toward 2027.

    CME Group operates the world's most diverse derivatives marketplace, offering trading for asset classes ranging from equities to energy and agriculture. The manufacturer generates revenue by charging fees for every contract traded and cleared on its platforms, serving professional traders, institutional investors, and central banks. In its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year 2025, the company noted that 85% of its derivatives contract volume came from exchange members.

    In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $6.5 billion, representing a growth rate of approximately 6.4% over the prior year. This revenue supported net income of close to $4 billion, resulting in a robust net margin of roughly 62%. The tech giant has consistently demonstrated the ability to convert trading volume into high levels of profit as global market volatility drives demand for its hedging tools.

    As of CME's December 2025 balance sheet, the company carries a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.1. This ratio measures total debt relative to shareholders' equity, indicating a conservative approach to borrowing. The current ratio, which compares short-term assets to short-term liabilities, is roughly 1. For the same period, free cash flow totaled nearly $4.2 billion. FCF represents the cash remaining after the business pays for its operating activities and capital expenditures.

    Sources indicate that toast provides an integrated cloud-based platform specifically designed for the restaurant industry, covering point-of-sale software and hardware. The firm primarily serves small and medium-sized businesses but is actively expanding into larger enterprise and mid-market restaurant segments. By the end of 2025, the company served over 170,000 locations across five countries, consolidating payments and operations into a single interface.

    In fiscal 2025, revenue reached approximately $6.2 billion, reflecting a rapid growth rate of roughly 24.1% over the previous year. The organization delivered net income of close to $342 million, achieving a net margin of nearly 5.6%. This performance marks a significant milestone, as the business transitioned from reporting annual losses to achieving sustainable profitability while continuing to gain market share.

    As of Toast's December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0, indicating the tech giant has negligible total debt relative to its equity. The current ratio stands at roughly 2.8, suggesting a strong ability to cover short-term obligations with liquid assets. Free cash flow for the period was nearly $608 million. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 36.6% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

    CME Group faces significant regulatory risk, particularly concerning potential upcoming laws governing digital assets and clearinghouse ownership structures. Competitive pressures are high from rival exchanges such as Intercontinental Exchange (ICE -0.80%) and Cboe Global Markets (CBOE -0.96%), along with emerging crypto platforms. The manufacturer also relies on licensing agreements with third-party providers like S&P Global (SPGI -2.34%), which could present risks if terms become unfavorable or exclusive access is lost.

    According to recent reports, toast is subject to an ongoing FTC lawsuit regarding the application of consumer protection acts to its business-to-business contracts. The organization relies heavily on Amazon (AMZN +0.33%) for its cloud infrastructure and third-party partners for payment processing and lending. Furthermore, the restaurant industry is highly susceptible to macroeconomic downturns, which could directly impact Toast's transaction volumes if consumer spending on dining falls.

    While Toast offers a significantly lower sales multiple, CME Group trades at a similar forward earnings premium despite its vastly superior net margin profile.

    Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

    The forward P/E uses future earnings estimates to determine whether a stock is priced fairly relative to its expected profits. The P/S ratio measures the market value of a company against its sales over the past 12 months.

    According to recent reports, CME Group and Toast are at very different stages in their respective business life cycles. CME Group is a mature, established organization, with a staggering net margin that would be the envy of most companies. It has undergone several iterations, but the original business is well over 100 years old.

    Meanwhile, Toast was founded just 14 years ago and only went public in 2021. So this is somewhat of an apples-to-oranges comparison.

    According to recent reports, since going public, Toast has been a disappointing investment. But in that same time frame, CME Group stock has barely outperformed the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.04%). CME does at least pay a modest dividend yielding about 1.6%. Toast has posted much stronger revenue growth recently, but I would expect that from an up-and-coming tech giant.

    In a recent development, I think the choice here comes down to your comfort with risk. A young firm like Toast is likely to have more growth opportunities ahead than a mature business like CME Group. But Toast is also less proven and faces significant competition from Square. I lean on the conservative side here: CME Group gets my vote for 2027 and beyond.

    #15998. Tech Report: I Didn’t Expect to Like Xiaomi’s Bizarre Dual-Screen Phone So Much

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2213 w)
    📖 Baca
    Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cnet ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: I Didn’t Expect to Like Xiaomi’s Bizarre Dual-Screen Phone So Much

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2213 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, xiaomi teased me with the 17 Pro, its bizarre dual-screen Android phone, last year.
    • It has been revealed that that sucks for Americans because this phone is actually damn good.
    • Beyond the screen, though, the 18 Pro Max packs the latest Qualcomm Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor, a fast-charging silicon-carbon battery and a potent camera setup that utilizes the same LOFIC sensor technology that impressed me so much in Xiaomi and Leica’s Leitzphone earlier this year.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, xiaomi teased me with the 17 Pro, its bizarre dual-screen Android phone, last year. But it was sold only in China. Being from the UK, I went back to my regular boring phone with its boring single screen. Significant sigh. So imagine my excitement when Xiaomi confirmed that its fresh flagship 18 Pro and Pro Max — complete with a second rear screen — would launch internationally, with a rollout including the UK and wider Europe. As with the rest of Xiaomi’s handsets, people in the US are flat out of luck.

    It has been revealed that that sucks for Americans because this phone is actually damn good. I worried that the rear screen would just be a dumb gimmick — something that tries to separate the phone from competitors but doesn’t actually add anything useful. But I actually like it. Need it? No. But it’s fun and has some genuine uses.

    Beyond the screen, though, the 18 Pro Max packs the latest Qualcomm Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor, a fast-charging silicon-carbon battery and a potent camera setup that utilizes the same LOFIC sensor technology that impressed me so much in Xiaomi and Leica’s Leitzphone earlier this year.

    According to recent reports, the 18 Pro isn’t just smaller (6.4 inches vs. the Pro Max’s 6.9 inches) it misses some of the Max’s top tech as well. The processor is a lesser model, the main camera doesn’t use LOFIC tech and the smaller battery isn’t as capable. Shame.

    But the 18 Pro Max is an all-round Android powerhouse, and I’ve really enjoyed getting to grips with it over the past couple of weeks. Here’s what I’ve found and what you need to know about this phone.

    According to recent reports, the extra display on the back is certainly this phone’s standout feature. It’s basically in the same place as the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera island, but instead of just being a piece of metal, it’s an actual functioning screen. If you’ve ever seen the cover display on a clamshell flip phone like Samsung’s Galaxy Z Flip 8, then it’ll seem quite familiar.

    Like the Flip 8, the second display shows incoming notifications, acting as a camera viewfinder and offering a variety of basic built-in functions like calendar reminders. What really hooked me, though, was the ability to create Gen AI apps just by typing in a prompt.

    For example, I asked for “a game where you just pop bubbles,” which the “Polish” tool elaborated on with deeper functions and visual styles before generating a finished game that was fully playable on the back screen, complete with a scoring system and, for some reason, a jellyfish mascot. It takes about 5 minutes for the app to be created each time, and its functions are limited. It’s not able to access any app data, so don’t expect to create a fresh email reader, and anything too technical will result in failure.

    I asked it to create a camera overlay that showed exposure settings (shutter speed, ISO and so on) to serve as a light meter for an analog camera. I’m not sure whether the issue was my explanation or a technical limitation, but it took the phone two tries to get something close. It created an interface with dials and exposure information, but it didn’t open the camera to calculate exposure as I’d hoped. As a result, it looked nice but it was functionally redundant.

    Another time, I asked it to create an app that highlighted real-time charging speeds. The resulting app showed current battery level but not charging speed. It did have a baffling “charging milestones completed” button that simply increased by one each time I tapped it. I also had no luck with my “rude word generator,” which just repeatedly came back with “Couldn’t generate.” Frustratingly, each time it fails to create an app, it doesn’t tell you why — like if you’re asking for information it’s unable to access — but just indicates to try again “in a minute or two,” which rarely resulted in success in my testing time. If I’m asking for something it can’t achieve, it’d be helpful to know that.

    Even so, I’m impressed with this app creation tool and, like many of the AI tools that only mildly excite me right now, I can only assume it will improve over time.

    Sources indicate that one of my favorite uses of the rear screen, though, is for vlogging. Firstly, seeing yourself from the back of the phone means you’re able to accurately film yourself using the best quality camera, rather than limiting yourself to the front-facing camera, which won’t look as good. But there’s also an autocue function where you can input a script and have it overlaid as text, allowing you to read out your words as you present to camera.

    It’s a powerful tool for vloggers and other video creators who rely on longer prewritten scripts for their videos. But it’s quite basic: the text simply auto-scrolls at a speed you set in advance. I’d love to see Xiaomi use voice recognition here to automatically progress the text as you read out the words, slowing down or speeding up as you naturally read aloud. This tech already exists, so I don’t think I’m asking for literal magic here.

    Sources indicate that tucked into that second display is a 200-megapixel main camera and a 200-megapixel telephoto camera offering 3.2x optical zoom or 6.4x hybrid zoom. There’s also a really tiny 50-megapixel ultrawide camera by itself below the camera island, which makes it feel like an afterthought — something that I’ll come back to later.

    According to recent reports, the main sensor is physically slightly smaller than the one in Xiaomi’s Leitzphone, but it uses the same LOFIC sensor tech for better dynamic range in a single image. I’ve taken a lot of photos with it so far and I’m really impressed with what I’ve seen. The smaller 18 Pro has an almost identical camera setup but its main sensor doesn’t use LOFIC, which is a shame as it forces you to go for the larger phone if you want the best possible image quality.

    Shots are well-exposed, with accurate colors and fine details that manage to look sharp but without the harsh over-sharpened look that’s all too often seen from phone cameras. Images look more natural as a result.

    Recent findings suggest that there are a lot of ways to tune your images in-camera — almost too many, in fact. There’s a whole host of built-in color presets, including a Leica-branded high-contrast black-and-white mode that I like, all of which you can customize further by adjusting the tones, colors, grain and white balance. Then there’s the option to shoot using the phone’s default color processing, going with “Leica Vibrant” for more popping colors or “Leica Authentic” for more natural tones. Each of these applies no matter what filter you then apply over the top.

    It has been revealed that confused? Yeah, I’m not entirely surprised, there are a lot of variables at play when taking an image with this thing but it didn’t take me long to figure out how to get the look that I wanted. And let’s be honest, there aren’t many photographers who want fewer options in how to take a photo.

    Then there’s Essential Moment, which is its own standalone mode where you can select from three distinct styles: a black and white mode, “modern vintage,” or “Iconic CCD.” Each of these is designed to replicate specific looks from cameras of the past, and Xiaomi says it uses AI to analyze the scene to authentically reproduce color tones, vintage lens effects and film grain (though crucially not generative AI to actually alter anything in the scene).

    It has been revealed that I actually love this, especially the black and white option, which produces monochrome images with beautiful contrast and genuinely authentic-looking film grain. It’s the mode I’d end up using most often, I’m sure, and I’ve taken a bunch of photos with it that I really like.

    Oh, and that tiny ultrawide camera, weirdly separated from its friends? It’s not great, with nighttime shots being particularly disappointing here. On the upside, the main camera’s standard focal length is 23mm, which is already pretty wide, so you probably won’t miss the ultrawide much.

    While the base 18 Pro uses Qualcomm’s latest Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, the Pro Max ups the ante with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. It’s no surprise that the Pro Max is a seriously powerful bit of kit, returning benchmark scores up there with the powerhouse Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra. Everything ran exceptionally smoothly, from playing demanding 3D games like Genshin Impact to editing photos or navigating the Android 17 interface. I found much the same with the 18 Pro, too — I didn’t see a noticeable difference in performance.

    Industry observers note that I don’t mind Xiaomi’s software skin, as it’s easy enough for anyone familiar with Android to get to grips with. What I don’t like, though, is the company’s insistence on preloading it with an armada of apps including AliExpress, Netflix, WPS Office, TikTok and others. Together with the variety of Xiaomi apps also on board, the phone feels somewhat cluttered before you’ve even had a chance to add anything of your own. I’ve seen worse examples (Oppo has been bad with this), but it still irks me that the phone ends up feeling almost like it’s ad-supported. And if it is, surely it should be cheaper?

    It has been revealed that the display has a “privacy mode” that uses hardware dimming to limit how much of the screen can be seen by people peeping over your shoulder. It’s similar to the tech we saw earlier this year on the Galaxy S26 Ultra, although having seen them both side by side, Samsung’s seems better. On the S26 Ultra, the privacy boost means that, when viewed off angle, content becomes essentially invisible. On the Xiaomi, while it looked much dimmer from the sides, I could still make out words on screen.

    It helps a bit, sure, but it won’t block those creeps entirely. My advice is: if you’ve got information so sensitive that even a glimpse would be career-ending, maybe wait until you’re alone before you put it on screen.

    Sources indicate that the 7,050-mAh silicon-carbon battery in the larger Pro Max packs a punch, putting in some solid scores on our demanding battery rundown tests. After one hour of YouTube streaming, it dropped to 97%, then to 89% after the third hour. That puts it above the Galaxy S26 Ultra and Google Pixel 11 Pro XL, although still below the current champion, the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

    According to recent reports, in everyday use, you won’t struggle to get through a full day of mixed use and you can likely be quite demanding with it and still not worry about it conking out mid-afternoon. Take photos, watch videos, listen to music – don’t stress over it; this thing should hold out fine.

    It has been revealed that the phone supports up to 100-watt wired fast charging, though you’ll need a Xiaomi fast charger to achieve the fastest speeds. I don’t have a Xiaomi charger (and the fastest it sells in the UK is 90W for £25), but I tried it with multiple third-party 100-watt chargers and the maximum I could get was around 65 watts. Even so, it went from 1% to 65% in 30 minutes of charging, which is still pretty quick — on par with the iPhone 18 Pro Max, in fact. Still, it should be able to go faster; you’ll just need to source a charger that will allow it.

    With its smaller 6,000-mAh battery the Xiaomi 18 Pro didn’t fare as well on our battery drain tests (it dropped to 93% after an hour of YouTube streaming) but in general use you’ll still comfortably get through most of a day on a single charge.

    Industry observers note that if you’re in the US, it’s something of a moot point. You can’t buy it. Sorry. Sure, you can probably import it from some third-party resellers, but it’s not officially on sale.

    If you’re somewhere where you can buy it, then lucky you — this phone is a blast. It ticks many of the boxes I’d expect from a flagship phone right now (camera quality in particular), and that second rear screen is the cherry on top. I expected it to feel like a pointless gimmick, and maybe it is a bit of a novelty, but it’s fun and I’ve already found it genuinely useful.

    Sources indicate that I don’t like that there are so many hardware differences between the two phone sizes, as it forces you to have a much bigger model if you want the best performance. I prefer Apple’s approach: With the iPhone 18 Pro, I can have the same exact potent camera setup and processor performance, no matter which size I choose. With Xiaomi’s phones I’m forced to compromise between performance and pocketability. If you want the best camera, then go for the bigger model. Battery life is better, too.

    Latest Update: Mortgage Rates Today, Monday, November 16: A Little Higher

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Yes, mortgage interest rates are higher today, but only by a little.
    • Industry observers note that the average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage rose to 7.27% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow.

    Yes, mortgage interest rates are higher today, but only by a little.

    Industry observers note that the average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage rose to 7.27% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is one basis point higher than yesterday and 37 basis points higher than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.).

    Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:.

    Recent findings suggest that mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

    On Friday, the Bureau of Labor Statistics released the Producer Price Index for October, which tracks the change in prices that U.S. producers are able to get for their products. This is one way to measure inflation on the market end, rather than the consumer end.

    The results were mixed. While prices didn’t rise quite as high as economists anticipated month-over-month (0.3% vs. 0.4%), year-over-year price growth did reach 6.5% — the largest increase in four years. This points to even higher costs for consumers coming in the near future.

    Investors are convinced that the Federal Reserve will raise overnight borrowing rates again in December to pull inflation down. And higher overnight borrowing rates — called the federal funds rate, which is what banks pay to fund products like mortgages — usually lead to higher mortgage rates.

    Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you blueprint to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

    Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

    If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

    There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

    If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

    Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

    According to recent reports, inflation data, earnings reports and tensions in the Middle East have been influencing the market. In this volatile backdrop, investors seeking income can bolster their portfolios by adding dividend-paying stocks.

    The recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help inform investors in their search for attractive stocks from the vast universe of dividend-paying companies. These experts assign ratings after analyzing a company's financials and ability to consistently pay dividends while also seeking capital appreciation.

    Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

    Integrated oil and gas giant Exxon Mobil has increased its dividends for 43 consecutive years. At a quarterly dividend of $1.03 per share (annualized dividend of $4.12), XOM stock offers a yield of 2.6%.

    In his latest research report on energy players, Morgan Stanley analyst Devin McDermott reiterated a buy rating on Exxon Mobil stock and increased his price target to $177 from $168.

    The analyst raised his free cash flow estimates to reflect Q2 guidance and the oil price strip, with the largest increase noted for integrated players due to higher refining margins. Notably, the five-star analyst raised his cash flow estimates by an average of 20% for the second half of 2026 and 7% for 2027.

    McDermott highlighted that while pure-play refiners have rallied on stronger margins, integrated energy stocks have lagged, creating relative-value opportunities in major North American integrated producers, including Exxon Mobil, Suncor and Cenovus Energy.

    Overall, McDermott is bullish on Exxon Mobil, as he expects the company to deliver strong earnings and cash flow growth, driven by robust upstream volumes, high-value projects in Product Solutions, and more than $5 billion of additional structural cost savings.

    "XOM's large global integrated operations and strong balance sheet (0.0x 2027 net leverage) make it a clear defensive play in an uncertain macro backdrop," stated McDermott.

    Sources indicate that mcDermott ranks No. 726 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 59% of the time, delivering an average return of 9.80%. See Exxon Mobil Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

    In a recent development, moving on to natural gas producer Expand Energy. The company announced a quarterly base dividend of $0.575 per share to be paid on Sept. 3. At an annualized dividend of $2.30 per share, EXE offers a yield of about 2.3%.

    Recently, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reaffirmed a buy rating on Expand Energy stock and increased his price target to $113 from $99. Mehta attributed his higher price target to cash flow improvement and a strong outlook for shareholder returns. He also cited the stock's attractive valuation, with an 11% free cash flow, or FCF, yield based on his 2027/2028 estimates compared with the peer average of 9%.

    Industry observers note that the five-star analyst expects Expand Energy to generate FCF per share of about $10 in FY28, up from the prior estimate of about $8 at his mid-cycle price forecast of $3.50/MMBtu Henry Hub. Mehta raised his FCF estimate to reflect an improved outlook for share repurchases, operational efficiencies, and gas pricing realizations.

    Furthermore, the analyst expects the recently revealed $1.25 billion Twin Eagle acquisition to enhance the competitive positioning of the combined business to expand to premium markets and capture incremental deals in the power and LNG end markets.

    Mehta ranks No. 449 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.1%. See Expand Energy Insider Trading on TipRanks.

    Mehta is also bullish on Diamondback Energy, an independent oil and natural gas company focused on energy reserves that are primarily in the Permian Basin in West Texas. The company recently paid a base cash dividend of $1.10 per share for the second quarter of 2026. FANG stock offers a dividend yield of 2.2%.

    Mehta increased his price target on FANG stock to $220 from $212 and reiterated a buy rating, citing the company's capital-efficient volume growth as oil prices remain high amid persistent supply disruption in the Middle East.

    "We remain constructive on FANG, a high-quality, pure-play Permian Basin operator that continues to drive incremental capital efficiencies and strong well productivity relative to peers," mentioned Mehta.

    Also, the analyst remarked that the removal of a minimum return of capital commitment gives Diamondback more flexibility in taking capital allocation decisions amid high oil price volatility and macro uncertainty.

    Mehta added that Diamondback sees a favorable environment for production growth, driven by the potential need for global inventory restocking. He highlighted that during Q2 2026, FANG's production volumes of 1,018 Mboe/d exceeded the high end of the tech giant's guidance, driven by a stronger-than-expected natural gas output from Barnett development and improved downstream gas marketing.

    Overall, Mehta is optimistic about Diamondback's growth and sees more upside in the stock, given higher production estimates, solid productivity and a deepening position in the Barnett shale formation. See Diamondback Energy Financials on TipRanks.

    It has been revealed that philadelphia 76ers forward Jaylen Brown briefly went down with a potential head injury after knocking heads with Brooklyn Nets forward Julius Randle. Though Brown was bleeding, he eventually returned to the game with a bandage on his head, and played a few more minutes of the 76ers' 135-123 win over the Nets.

    It has been revealed that the collision between Brown and Randle happened in the fourth quarter of Monday's matchup in Brooklyn, with Brown's forehead connecting with Randle's mouth. Both men were bleeding after the incident, though from different parts of the head.

    Recent findings suggest that brown stayed down for a while, rolling onto his back and covering his face with his hands. The entire 76ers bench soon came out to surround him while he was tended to by trainers. Brown then received additional care on the bench, before returning to the game with a bandage on his head.

    Brown eventually left again because of tightness in his left hamstring. He noted he will have additional testing on both his head and his hamstring on Tuesday.

    Randle, meanwhile, got his bloody lip stitched up off the court and returned to the game as well. Randle was called for the foul on the play, but because it wasn't a shooting foul, Brown did not need to attempt free throws.

    According to recent reports, at the time of the foul, Brown had scored 29 points and picked up 12 rebounds, thanks to a first-half double-double. He finished with 31 points, 13 rebounds and 4 assists in the 12-point victory.

    Joel Embiid led both teams with 37 points, while Randle had 33 points for Brooklyn in the loss.

    It has been revealed that TL;DR: Pokémon GO and Duolingo just teamed up for exclusive cross-app rewards. Score free Duolingo avatar suits, regional and shiny encounters, and more.

    Pokémon GO and Duolingo just merged forces in one of the most delightfully chaotic app crossovers of the year.

    Recent findings suggest that live from Nov. 17, the two mobile giants are running a cross-app event called Duo’s Pokémon Party. By keeping a seven-day language streak alive in Duolingo, players can unlock custom Pokémon outfits for their Duolingo avatars alongside a unique promo code for event-themed Timed Research in Pokémon GO.

    To join, trainers must opt into Duo’s Pokémon Party inside the Duolingo app by Dec. 21, and finish at least one lesson per day across seven separate days before Dec. 29. It's that easy.

    Maybe we're cynical, but this feels like a rare opportunity. It's refreshing to see a free cross-promotion that rewards daily habits across both platforms:.

    Four free Duolingo avatar suits: Completing daily lessons unlocks up to nine total rewards, headlined by four wearable Pokémon suits for your Duolingo profile: Pikachu, Chatot, a Poké Ball, and a Pokémon GO trainer outfit.

    Regional and Shiny encounters in Pokémon GO: Finishing seven days of lessons generates a unique offer code redeemable on the Pokémon GO Web Store. That unlocks Timed Research featuring XP, Stardust, and guaranteed encounters with Pikachu, Meowth, Lucario, and regional-exclusive Chatot.

    Recent findings suggest that foreign-language gameplay and latest language tags: When you activate the Timed Research, you pick a target language, and your tasks actually appear in that language. Caught Pokémon also debut a new Language Tag on their summary screen, letting you tap to inspect their official names across different languages.

    Recent findings suggest that we should note that while the Pokémon GO encounters are permanent additions to your Pokédex, the four Pokémon avatar suits are temporary rentals. All earned Pokémon suits will automatically expire and vanish from your Duolingo closet on March 31, 2027.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    What if your phone had a second display on the back?

    It has been revealed that if you've asked yourself this question, or have peered lustfully at the newly introduced foldable phones, including from Apple, you should take a look at the new Xiaomi 18 Pro or 18 Pro Max. The display is very cool and does bring some functionality that you otherwise just cannot have, though it's not nearly as versatile as what you get with a foldable phone.

    I've spent a few days with both phones, and I can tell you, these are incredibly fast, capable, and sleek devices, albeit a little iPhone-like. The display on the back is what makes them stand out from the crowd, at least visually, but it's not something that will drastically change the way you use your phone.

    It has been revealed that the Xiaomi 18 Pro series is not Xiaomi's first phone to feature a secondary display on the back; last year's Xiaomi 17 Pro had one, too. Just like the main display on the front, it hasn't changed much since last year: It's still a 2.9-inch, 596x976 pixel AMOLED display, though it is a little brighter than before. I didn't get to try the 17 Pro, though, so the display on the back is latest to me.

    Displays: 6.9-inch, 1,208x2,624 pixel, 120Hz AMOLED display with 4000 nits of peak brightness; secondary display on the back: 2.9-inch, 120Hz AMOLED display with 4000 nits of peak brightness.

    Design: Dragon Crystal Glass 3 front, aluminum frame,.

    Size and weight: 163.4 x 77.6 x 8.4 mm; weight: 240 grams.

    Rear cameras: A triple rear camera system with a 200-megapixel, f/1.7 wide camera, a 200-megapixel, f/2.4 periscope telephoto camera, and a 50-megapixel, f/2.4 ultrawide camera.

    Front cameras: 50-megapixel, f/2.2 selfie camera.

    Processor: Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6.

    Storage: 256GB/512GB/1TB with 12/16GB of RAM.

    Battery life: 7,050mAh battery with 100W charging, 50 wireless, and 27W reverse wireless charging.

    Software: Android 17, HyperOS 4.

    Water and dust resistance: IP68 rating.

    Special features: Under display ultrasonic fingerprint scanner, stereo audio system with 3 speakers, 24-bit/192kHz hi-res audio support.

    Yes, this is an extremely powerful phone, even though it isn't technically Xiaomi's flagship (that's the Ultra series, which isn't out yet this year). You get the latest Snapdragon chip, a massive camera upgrade over last year's 50-megapixel system, and a humongous battery that charges very rapidly.

    The Xiaomi 18 Pro, which I also received for testing but have spent less time with, has a 6.4-inch display, a smaller battery, with the rest being mostly the same.

    Industry observers note that xiaomi flagships in the numbered series follow the same philosophy: Make a phone that's very much like an iPhone, but stuff it with extremely powerful hardware for added value. It starts with the phones' names (18 Pro and 18 Pro Max), it's visible in parts of the design, and Xiaomi's HyperOS, which has been upgraded to version 4 here, can be set up to mirror iOS in almost every way.

    This is not a bad thing. The Xiaomi 18 Pro is distinctive enough with its dual display that overall iPhone-likeness doesn't feel like you're having a cheap copy. And I don't mind the HyperOS software being a dead ringer for iOS, down to the near-identical Control Center (which, you guessed it, is called the Control Center on the Xiaomi as well).

    Recent findings suggest that do I need a display on the back of the phone? Not really. It's useful for photos as it can give cues to the folks you're photographing, and it can take your selfies game to the next level as you can actually take selfies with the 200-megapixel main camera system. Other than that, it just looks cool.

    Industry observers note that but you do need to see it in real life to appreciate just how cool it is. It's an excellent, super-bright, pixel-dense AMOLED display with a 120Hz refresh rate. I set it up with an ocean wave animation that looks downright beautiful when I touch it. You can have AI-based apps on there, and even use it for simple games. It's so good that I kept consciously placing the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max on its face when setting it on a table, just to appreciate the crispness of that mini display on the back.

    Recent findings suggest that but other than the camera tricks, it's still (surprise!) preferable to use the much larger front display for most tasks. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

    The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

    And yes, the 6.9-inch front display is excellent, too: Silky smooth, plenty bright, and it even has a Privacy Display option, similar to the one on recent Samsung flagships.

    Recent findings suggest that up until a few years ago, battery capacities north of 5,000mAh were reserved for thick specialty phones focusing on battery life. But then a couple of battery breakthroughs (including silicon-carbon battery tech which Xiaomi is using here) made it to the mass market, and now Xiaomi can place an 7,050mAh battery in the regular-sized Xiaomi 18 Pro Max.

    The battery charges quickly on a fast charger and it lasts for at least two days. It's so good that I didn't have proper time to really test it as I only charged the phone twice in little under a week.

    I don't think I've ever used a Xiaomi phone that was as quick and worked as smoothly as this one. Everything I touched opened instantly (including the fingerprint scanner which takes a tiny fraction of a second to analyze your digit and log you in). Playing with animated, AI-based and fancy perspective wallpapers did not punish me in terms of speed, as the phone kept operating incredibly smoothly.

    Yes, it has the latest Snapdragon chip inside, but I guess Xiaomi also polished its HyperOS 4 to make it a little speedier than before.

    As is customary for Xiaomi, HyperOS does have a maddening number of features and options, some of which are tucked away in some menu you wouldn't think of. But given the versatility of this phone, it's hard to blame them. One I set the phone up as I liked, the complexity of the Settings did not bother me.

    We've gotten to a point in which Xiaomi can put two 200-megapixel cameras, and a two 50-megapixel ones on a phone that's not really their camera flagship.

    Do we need so many megapixels? Possibly not, as evidenced in the fact that Xiaomi 18 Pro Max takes 12.5 megapixel photos by default, and you have to manually up the resolution to either 50 or 200 megapixels.

    Recent findings suggest that but the high megapixel count opens up interesting possibilities, such as zooming in at 12.8x without losing quality. The telephoto camera doubles as a macro camera that can go in really close (its minimum focusing distance is 12 centimetres), with Xiaomi calling it a "telescope and microscope in one.".

    I haven't had enough time with the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's camera to fully assess how good it is. From what I've seen, though, it's an incredibly versatile and powerful system that you can use to squeeze out a good photo in almost every scenario.

    In a recent development, the Xiaomi 18 Pro starts at 1,399 EUR, while the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max starts at 1,599 EUR in Europe. The colors on offer are Cosmic Blue, Black, White, and Velvet Red for both devices. We don't have the exact date of availability yet, and will update this article when we get them.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If I could only own three exchange-traded funds (ETFs) for the rest of my life, I'd want a combination that could serve me through every stage of investing.
    • I also wouldn't want to spend much time managing the portfolio.
    • Recent findings suggest that three ETFs that meet those requirements are the Schwab U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If I could only own three exchange-traded funds (ETFs) for the rest of my life, I'd want a combination that could serve me through every stage of investing. That means owning companies capable of growing my wealth, generating an increasing stream of dividend income, and providing diversification across industries and geographies.

    I also wouldn't want to spend much time managing the portfolio. I'd prefer funds I could buy regularly and hold for decades.

    Recent findings suggest that three ETFs that meet those requirements are the Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF (SCHD -0.39%), Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF (VTI -0.21%), and Vanguard Morningstar Total International Stock ETF (VXUS -0.60%).

    It has been revealed that the Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF passively tracks the Dow Jones U.S. Dividend 100 Index, which measures the performance of 100 of the highest-quality, high-yielding dividend growth stocks. It screens companies based on yield, five-year dividend growth rate, and financial strength.

    That dual focus on yield and growth is worth noting. Over the last 50 years, dividend growers in the S&P 500 have delivered higher total returns with less volatility than companies that don't pay dividends, hold their payouts flat, and cut or eliminate their dividends. That has made dividend growers an ideal way to grow wealth over the long term.

    NYSEMKT · As of 9:58 AM ET 11/17/26.

    SCHD has delivered strong total returns since its inception in 2011 (13.8% annualized). Meanwhile, it currently offers an attractive dividend yield (around 3%, nearly triple the S&P 500's level). That growing income stream will become increasingly important when I retire. These features make this ETF a great core holding for those seeking rising income while still growing their wealth.

    It has been revealed that the Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF is a great complement to SCHD because it adds exposure to companies that don't meet its dividend requirements. This fund owns the entire U.S. stock market. It provides exposure to large, medium, and small companies, as well as to growth, value, and income stocks. VTI at the moment holds over 3,500 companies.

    NYSEMKT · As of 9:56 AM ET 11/17/26.

    Recent findings suggest that the fund weights its holdings by market cap, resulting in a higher allocation to the largest publicly traded companies. Presently, most of the country's largest stocks are tech companies, which gives this ETF a higher weighting to that sector at nearly 40% of its assets. For comparison, tech accounts for only about 12% of SCHD's holdings.

    According to recent reports, VTI is an ideal foundational ETF to hold in any portfolio. It will provide returns that match those of the entire stock market. While its current higher allocation to tech stocks could make it more volatile, tech stocks are also the economy's main growth driver and could help drive this ETF's returns over the coming years.

    The Vanguard Total International Stock Market ETF provides something both SCHD and VTI lack: International exposure. This ETF tracks the investment returns of companies outside the U.S. It provides exposure to both developed markets (e.g., Europe) and emerging markets (e.g., India and China).

    NASDAQ · As of 9:57 AM ET 11/17/26.

    The ETF right now holds about 8,875 stocks. While it also weights holdings by market cap, its top 10 holdings account for less than 13% of the total. That compares to 33% for VTI. Meanwhile, VXUS' top holdings include technology, healthcare, energy, and financial stocks, while nine of VTI's top holdings are tech-related companies. So, you're getting much more diversification from this ETF, both by industry and geography.

    Industry observers note that adding VXUS to the mix would reduce a portfolio's dependence on U.S. market valuations, economic conditions, and corporate earnings. However, it does add newly introduced risks, including currency, political, and regulatory risks. That's a worthwhile trade-off for greater diversification benefits.

    If I could only own three ETFs for the rest of my life, SCHD, VTI, and VXUS would be my picks. Together, they provide an attractive combination of dividend quality, long-term growth potential, and international diversification. That combination should help grow my wealth. While I'd still want some cash and bonds as I approach retirement, these three ETFs could serve as the foundation of my equity portfolio for decades to come.
