    #15969. The Chief Architect As The Enterprise Orchestra Conductor

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1008 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    The Chief Architect As The Enterprise Orchestra Conductor

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1008 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Robert Sheesley is an award-winning executive, speaker and author, known for technology-enabled transformation and new value creation.
    • An orchestra can assemble extraordinary musicians and still deliver an uneven performance.
    • Enterprises face the same challenge.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Robert Sheesley is an award-winning executive, speaker and author, known for technology-enabled transformation and new value creation.

    An orchestra can assemble extraordinary musicians and still deliver an uneven performance. Every section may play its own part beautifully, yet the composition suffers when timing, interpretation and balance fail to come together.

    Enterprises face the same challenge. Talented people, strong business units and substantial technology investments do not automatically produce strong enterprise results. Departments pursue reasonable objectives, projects meet their delivery milestones and new technologies arrive with compelling promises. Customers and employees experience how those contributions fit together.

    The chief architect helps shape that collective performance. Working across organizational boundaries, the architect connects strategic intent to the capabilities, investments and operating changes required to deliver it. AI extends this responsibility by introducing new ways to understand the enterprise and new participants in its work.

    The conductor metaphor is useful because it places architecture where it belongs: close to the relationship, between strategy and execution.

    A conductor understands the full score, listens across sections and helps specialists contribute to a shared interpretation. The chief architect brings a comparable perspective to the enterprise, helping leaders see how their decisions affect the whole.

    It has been revealed that business leaders retain accountability for results. Executives determine strategic priorities and authorize investments. The architect contributes the enterprise design, evidence and coordination needed to make those choices workable.

    According to recent reports, A strategic ambition such as improving customer loyalty or increasing operational efficiency leaves considerable room for interpretation. Different business units can pursue the same ambition through incompatible investments.

    In a recent development, the chief architect helps make the intended outcome explicit. What must customers experience differently? Which business capabilities must improve? What changes in information, processes, technology and employee skills would make that improvement possible?

    Recent findings suggest that kaplan and Norton’s work on strategy maps provides a useful foundation. It connects organizational capabilities and internal processes with customer and financial outcomes. Those connections express management’s reasoning about how investment should create value. They also give the enterprise assumptions it can test through execution.

    For example, a company seeking greater customer loyalty might propose faster service resolution. Achieving that outcome could require better diagnostic knowledge, reliable access to customer history, clearer authority for resolving exceptions and additional employee training.

    Architecture makes these relationships visible before the enterprise commits to a solution.

    Business capabilities describe what the enterprise must be able to do, such as manage suppliers, fulfill orders, develop products or resolve customer issues. They provide a useful basis for discussion across departments because they remain recognizable even as reporting structures and systems change.

    The chief architect uses that perspective to connect strategy with investment. Leaders can examine the capabilities their objectives depend on, assess current performance and identify gaps that deserve attention.​.

    A strategy becomes consequential when leaders allocate capital, talent and management attention.

    Sources indicate that the technology investment board adds an essential dimension to the conductor metaphor. It provides a forum for evaluating investments across the enterprise, balancing priorities, risk and forecasted return, and provides for mechanisms to properly evaluate and adjust the portfolio as conditions change.

    The chief architect brings the architectural evidence into that conversation: capability gaps, shared dependencies, reuse opportunities, accumulated debt and the consequences of sequencing decisions. Portfolio management contributes delivery and resource information. Finance helps assess affordability and benefits. Business sponsors explain the operational changes required to realize value.

    Together, these perspectives support decisions about what to fund, defer, reshape or stop.

    A balanced portfolio must sustain current operations while improving performance and developing future capabilities. Required security or compliance work may have limited discretionary choice. Foundational investments may enable several later initiatives without producing an immediate standalone return.

    Architecture helps make those relationships explicit. A shared data capability, for example, may support customer service, planning and multiple AI applications. Evaluating it only within one project could understate its contribution. Counting its full benefits in every dependent project could overstate the portfolio’s return.

    The architect helps leaders understand the common foundation and allocate costs and benefits consistently.

    Timing matters just as much as selection. Several individually attractive projects can overwhelm the same subject matter experts, compete for integration capacity or require employees to absorb too much change at once. A credible portfolio accounts for the enterprise’s ability to perform the work.

    AI contributes to this operating model in two ways.

    First, it can strengthen architectural work. With appropriate access and validation, AI can help examine documentation, identify possible dependencies, compare designs and summarize evidence for investment reviews. These capabilities can reduce the effort required to investigate a complex enterprise.

    The resulting analysis still needs scrutiny. Missing information can produce incomplete maps. Recommendations can overlook operational constraints. Forecasts depend on the quality of their data and assumptions.

    The chief architect establishes how that evidence will be checked and how much confidence a decision should place in it.

    Second, AI becomes part of business execution. Assistants help employees interpret information. Models support forecasts. Agents can perform defined actions within workflows.

    It has been revealed that leaders must decide who owns the outcome, what authority AI receives and how people detect and address failure. Adding AI to a fragmented process can increase the speed at which fragmentation produces consequences.

    Ultimately, the chief architect earns the conductor’s role by helping the enterprise turn strategic intent into a coordinated, measurable performance. Business architecture identifies the capabilities that matter; investment governance directs resources toward them; process management connects those capabilities through the daily work that delivers customer value.

    AI can strengthen this performance by informing decisions, supporting people and executing appropriate tasks within clearly defined boundaries. Its contribution depends on sound process design, accountable business ownership and feedback that guides continuous improvement.

    The chief architect keeps these relationships in view, helping leaders judge success through better customer outcomes, stronger operational performance and the enterprise’s growing ability to adapt and learn.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, palantir Technologies (PLTR -0.29%) has been a successful long-term investment since its 2020 IPO.
    • It is often the case that raised guidance leads to an improved stock price, but this latest report was different.
    • It has been revealed that why is that?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, palantir Technologies (PLTR -0.29%) has been a successful long-term investment since its 2020 IPO. That’s largely because it is also a successful business, as evidenced by its artificial intelligence platform, which has been widely adopted in both commercial and government settings. Palantir continues to outperform expectations, both externally and internally, and management has raised its annual guidance at every quarterly report this year.

    It is often the case that raised guidance leads to an improved stock price, but this latest report was different. Palantir's stock price actually fell following its Q3 earnings, and the tech giant is now posting negative returns for the year.

    It has been revealed that why is that? I think one figure holds the clue.

    Industry observers note that every investor loves a good beat-and-raise quarter, but when that becomes the expectation, it loses its effectiveness. The market now expects Palantir to matter soft guidance each quarter and beat those expectations. After a while, this becomes the status quo for investors, and they demand bigger beats and raises because the original beat and raise have become the baseline.

    NASDAQ · As of 9:57 AM ET 11/17/26.

    But Palantir has another matter going on with its stock. While its growth rate was an impressive 96% year over year in Q3, the reality is that its stock has already priced in much of that growth. Shares also fell because of investor concerns about slowing growth in total contract value. The report was also released on a generally bad day for the market and got caught up in the sell-off.

    Palantir is one of the most expensive stocks on the market, trading at over 100 times forward earnings and 68 times next year's earnings estimate. And that’s even after this latest sell-off.

    PLTR PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts.

    You'd be hard-pressed to find another stock trading at that level in the AI realm, which puts Palantir in a class of its own. Sometimes being an outlier like this is a significant problem, as it could lead to Palantir's valuation declining to a more reasonable level over the next year.

    Sources indicate that most of Palantir's peers are trading at 20 to 40 times next year's earnings, which means that even if Palantir hits next year's expectations squarely, the stock would need to decline by at least 40% to be in a reasonable valuation range with its peers. That's the harsh reality of Palantir's stock, as so much growth is already priced in. This means investors may need to get used to underperformance for a while.

    #15965. The Hidden Costs Of DIY AI: Why The Real Expense Begins After The Prototype

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1048 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    The Hidden Costs Of DIY AI: Why The Real Expense Begins After The Prototype

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1048 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sundar Balasubramanian is Senior Vice President of Product Management at Icertis.
    • ​Artificial intelligence (AI) has created the false impression that enterprise software has become remarkably inexpensive to build.
    • Industry observers note that what many organizations often underestimate is that the prototype is the easiest part of the journey.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sundar Balasubramanian is Senior Vice President of Product Management at Icertis.

    ​Artificial intelligence (AI) has created the false impression that enterprise software has become remarkably inexpensive to build. In many ways, that perception is justified. Business teams can now create applications, agents, workflows and copilots in a matter of days or weeks instead of months. Capabilities that once required large development teams and technical expertise are now accessible through natural language prompts and off-the-shelf AI services.

    Industry observers note that what many organizations often underestimate is that the prototype is the easiest part of the journey. The real challenge begins when AI applications become business-critical and require ongoing governance, support, security, maintenance, model management and operational accountability over time.

    As companies rush to build AI-powered solutions, they are discovering that while the economics of creating software have changed dramatically, the economics of operating enterprise software have not. Reliability, accountability, governance, support and continuous improvement remain essential requirements. The difference is that organizations often encounter these realities later in the process, after the excitement of rapid deployment has taken hold.

    It has been revealed that one of the most exciting aspects of AI is the speed at which teams can transform an idea into a working application. This capability has unlocked a newly introduced wave of experimentation across the enterprise. Departments that previously relied on centralized development resources can now create solutions tailored to their own needs, accelerating innovation and expanding access to technology.

    But leaders should be careful not to confuse a successful pilot with a scalable enterprise solution. An application serving a small group of users within a single department operates in a relatively controlled environment. The requirements change significantly when that same solution is expected to support thousands of employees across multiple business units, regions and regulatory environments. At that point, reliability becomes a critical business requirement.

    This is where many organizations encounter an unexpected reality: Scaling an AI solution introduces more complexity than building it in the first place. What begins as a low-cost experiment can become a long-term operational commitment, requiring sustained investment in maintenance, support and continuous improvement as the business evolves.​.

    Industry observers note that organizations not only have to maintain the technology itself, but also ensure the expertise required to keep it effective. AI models, technologies and business requirements continue to evolve. Therefore, keeping pace requires ongoing investment in specialized skills, research and development, and product improvement long after the initial AI tool is deployed. This is one reason many organizations rely on specialized software providers rather than building everything themselves. They gain access to teams whose primary responsibility is staying ahead of technological change, benefitting from expertise and best practices developed across a broader customer ecosystem. Perhaps most importantly, they establish long-term accountability for support, product evolution and continuity.

    Recent findings suggest that contract lifecycle management is a timely example of where the economics of building and operating often diverge. AI can accelerate the creation of contract review tools, clause extraction workflows or conversational interfaces. What is less visible is the ongoing investment required to support a system that manages sensitive commercial data, integrates with enterprise systems and provides the business context needed for AI to deliver reliable, actionable outcomes. These costs extend far beyond maintenance alone and appear in places organizations least expect.

    AI has introduced a fundamentally different cost structure than traditional enterprise software. Consumption, utilization and optimization matter now more than ever before as the economics of how AI is deployed become just as vital as what it can do. Specialized software is engineered to address business requirements at enterprise scale, while minimizing token spend.

    Generalized AI applications, in comparison, can turn what appears to be a modest operating cost into a substantial recurring expense as usage grows because they are not purpose-built for the complex, high-volume processes of an enterprise.

    AI consumption has already become a boardroom discussion, shaping budgeting, governance and long-term planning in much the same way that cloud computing did. Many organizations initially focused on the flexibility and speed cloud platforms provided, only to discover later that ongoing consumption required deliberate oversight to keep costs aligned with business outcomes. As adoption scales, organizations need to consider not just where AI is being used, but how to apply it most efficiently for the needs of their business.

    Sources indicate that many organizations approach governance as something that must be addressed before deployment. Policies are established. Reviews are conducted. Controls are defined. Once those steps are complete, there can be a tendency to assume the governance challenge has been solved.

    In a recent development, in reality, governance often becomes more key after deployment than before it. Once employees begin relying on AI to support decisions and workflows, newly introduced questions inevitably arise. Who owns the application? Who approves modifications to prompts or underlying models? How should outputs be monitored and evaluated? What metrics should be used to measure performance and business value?

    According to recent reports, these are not questions that can be answered once and forgotten. They require continuous attention. Governance evolves from a compliance-oriented exercise into an operational discipline focused on ensuring that controls remain effective as technology, regulations and business requirements continue to change.

    Sources indicate that governance also carries direct cost implications. Without clear ownership and oversight, organizations can encounter duplicated solutions, inconsistent outputs, excessive model usage and unexpected expenses associated with resolving complications related to accuracy, security or compliance. What initially appears to be a faster path to innovation can ultimately create inefficiencies that erode the value the initiative was intended to deliver.

    Organizations that underestimate this responsibility may find themselves devoting far more time and resources to managing governance than they anticipated when building the original solution.

    The broader lesson, however, is that AI has changed the cost of building software, but it has not eliminated the responsibilities that come with operating enterprise technology. The most successful organizations look beyond the speed of development and evaluate AI through a total cost of ownership lens. The prototype may be inexpensive. The real investment begins when the solution becomes part of how the business runs.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that shares of Costco Wholesale (COST +0.38%) have been surging recently, hitting new all-time highs. After the manufacturer revealed yet another special dividend, many investors rushed to invest in the company. On Monday, the stock closed at over $1,113, with its year-to-date gains now sitting at nearly 30%.

    Recent findings suggest that while the business itself is solid, Costco's stock certainly isn't cheap. Buying it now will involve paying a hefty premium, which can be risky for investors. Is the stock worth buying right now, to lock in the special dividend, or is it simply too expensive?

    In a recent development, last week, Costco revealed that it will pay a special cash dividend of $30 to its shareholders. Anyone who is a shareholder of record as of the end of Nov. 24 will be eligible for the payment on Dec. 4.

    In a recent development, costco has issued special dividend payments in the past, with the most recent one being announced in 2023. That payment, however, was $15. This upcoming one is significantly more, and it's a big deal for a stock that right now pays a quarterly dividend of just $1.47, or $5.88 over the course of a full year. The $30 special dividend is effectively the equivalent of more than five years of dividends at the current rate; for dividend investors, there's a huge incentive to buy the stock for the payout.

    The danger, of course, is that as dividend investors load up on the stock for the payout, they may also drop it soon afterward, and thus, the stock could end up falling and giving back its recent gains.

    NASDAQ · As of 9:59 AM ET 11/17/26.

    In a recent development, while it would be great to lock in such a high dividend right now and take advantage of a large one-time payment, it amounts to less than a 3% return given the stock's inflated value. Meanwhile, the risk is that after the special dividend, it could easily fall more than that. This is, after all, a stock that is trading at a whopping 54 times its trailing earnings. The average S&P 500 stock trades at a multiple of just 23.

    In a recent development, it may sound like easy money to buy now for the dividend, but given the downside risk here, the special dividend isn't enough to tempt me to buy such an overpriced stock. There are better buying opportunities out there, stocks that can easily rise more than 3% and that also offer better upside for investors in the long run.

Not many investors would likely have predicted that to be the case even a few years ago, as its former CEO Warren Buffett was largely hesitant to invest in tech (aside from Apple) and in areas outside his expertise.

    Industry observers note that the substantial question is whether Nvidia (NVDA -0.18%) will also find its way into Berkshire's portfolio. It certainly checks off a lot of boxes right now.

    Recent findings suggest that nvidia is precisely the type of organization that Berkshire might invest in if it were comfortable with tech, and more specifically, artificial intelligence (AI). Nvidia has a strong moat, as tech companies rely on its cutting-edge chips for AI development. It dominates market share, and that enables it to charge high prices and post excellent profit margins.

    Now, with the stock also falling sharply after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO and president, its lower valuation could make it a far more appealing buy. Trading at around just 10 times its expected future profits (based on analyst estimates), it looks like a bargain buy right now. If Berkshire's management is indeed taking a more favorable approach to tech, Nvidia might just be a slam-dunk buy.

And if Berkshire also invests in Nvidia, that could signal to investors that tech will be a key part of its long-term strategy.

    Industry observers note that for investors who have been craving more growth and aggressiveness from Berkshire's management, this could be a welcome change. The same may not be true, however, for investors who prefer a more cautious approach.

    Investors may want to wait a few months to see whether Berkshire has indeed invested in Nvidia, as that will make it clear whether investing in tech will be the fresh norm moving forward.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    The Next Great Infrastructure Reset

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Rajjie Sarmey is Founder and Chief Visionary Officer of FutureProof CXO, advancing governed AI, enterprise strategy and durable value.
    • It has been revealed that the next great enterprise infrastructure reset may not begin inside a data center.
    • Recent findings suggest that for decades, enterprise technology strategy centered around computing capacity, consolidation, connectivity, virtualization and cloud migration.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rajjie Sarmey is Founder and Chief Visionary Officer of FutureProof CXO, advancing governed AI, enterprise strategy and durable value.

    It has been revealed that the next great enterprise infrastructure reset may not begin inside a data center. It could begin beneath an ocean, at an electrical substation, along a telecommunications corridor or within an orbital network. Its consequences could cascade all four domains.

    Recent findings suggest that for decades, enterprise technology strategy centered around computing capacity, consolidation, connectivity, virtualization and cloud migration. We optimized utilization, negotiated consumption economics, reduced technical debt and pursued geographic scale and redundancy. Those disciplines remain essential today but are now insufficient.

    As we navigate the remainder of 2026 and prepare for 2030, the strategic question shifts from where enterprises compute most efficiently to where they can operate securely, safely, reliably, lawfully and economically when interconnected infrastructure assumptions fail.

    I define this emerging discipline as Infrastructure-Consequence Economics—a fundamental shift in how boards, CXOs, investors and architects evaluate digital infrastructure.

    Three documented indicators reveal this transition.

    1. Electricity is becoming a strategic computing constraint. The International Energy Agency’s 2025 “Energy and AI” report projected global data center electricity consumption rising from approximately 415 TWh in 2024 to 945 TWh by 2030 under its base-case scenario, acknowledging significant uncertainty in the future.​.

    2. Infrastructure is entering an extraordinary capital cycle. McKinsey estimated in April 2025 that data centers would require approximately $6.7 trillion in cumulative worldwide capital by 2030, encompassing AI and conventional computing workloads.​.

    It has been revealed that 3. Digital globalization depends on concentrated physical connectivity. A 2025 International Telecommunication Union report highlighted that submarine cables carried more than 99% of international data flows.​.

    These projections aren’t guarantees, but they signal increasing interdependencies. Converging capital intensity, energy availability, physical connectivity and geopolitical risk are now reshaping enterprise computing economics.

    In a recent development, submarine cables connect geographies, financial markets, cloud environments and global commerce. A multiregional cloud architecture may still depend on shared cable corridors, telecom providers and/or landing stations. Geographic separation doesn’t guarantee dependency independence.

    AI demands dependable electricity, transmission capacity, cooling, water where applicable, network connectivity, physical security and suitable locations. Available compute without sufficient power delivery isn’t deployable capacity.

    As we race toward 2030, infrastructure readiness and energy availability may influence workload placement as significantly as processor performance or cloud pricing.

    Sources indicate that aviation communications, wireless networks and airborne platforms extend operations beyond terrestrial infrastructure. Across aviation, distributed industries, logistics and emergency response aspects, resilience demands managing spectrum, coverage, backhaul and continuity risks.

    Mission-critical connectivity depends on coordinated terrestrial, airborne and satellite capabilities and not isolated networks or assumed independence.

    Satellite communications and positioning, combined with navigation and timing services, strengthen operational continuity when terrestrial systems fail but introduce distinct risks that involves interference, cybersecurity, terminal dependencies, service concentration and regulatory constraints. Resilience architecture must extend into the physical and jurisdictional systems supporting them.

    Recent findings suggest that decades of leading transformations across mission-critical regulated environments reinforces one principle: Redundancy isn’t resilience when independent systems share common failure points. Multiple cloud providers, facilities and backup ecosystems may share critical dependencies across identity, security, power, telecom and operations.

    Sources indicate that resilience is measured not by provider count but by the ability to sustain or restore critical business services within defined risk and recovery tolerances. It mandates mapped dependencies, independent recovery paths, tested failovers, well-defined decision authority and verifiable recoverability. In high-risk environments, resilience must be demonstrated, not merely documented.

    According to recent reports, traditionally, infrastructure economics focus on acquisition costs, capacity, consumption, utilization and operating efficiency. These measures remain necessary but rarely capture the full economic impact of infrastructure failure, prolonged disruption, geographic concentration or sovereign restrictions.

    I propose evaluating infrastructure decisions through five interconnected dimensions:.

    In a recent development, 1. Economic Sustainability: Full life cycle costs across capital, compute, energy, networking, cooling and operations.

    2. Dependency Resilience: Exposure to correlated failures across facilities, providers, utilities and networks.

    Industry observers note that 3. Jurisdictional Assurance: Data residency, contractual enforceability, regulatory obligations and operational control.

    4. Recoverability: Demonstrated restoration capabilities, RTOs and RPOs, and service continuity.

    In a recent development, 5. Trusted Business Outcomes: Measurable value within defined security, reliability, safety and risk tolerances.

    Recent findings suggest that the governing principle is to optimize not for the lowest infrastructure unit price but for risk-adjusted cost per trusted business outcomes. Every material infrastructure investment should be evaluated against its life cycle economics, correlated failure risks, tested recoverability, jurisdictional obligations and measurable business consequences.

    For boards, the question is whether executive leadership understands the infrastructure dependencies, capital exposures and failure scenarios that could compromise enterprise investments. For CXOs, architecture must connect business criticality, recovery engineering, workload positioning, cybersecurity and economic accountability.

    According to recent reports, for investors, infrastructure valuations demand scrutiny beyond unveiled compute capacity, meaning power availability, utilization, customer commitments, financing costs and monetization assumptions. For founders, the strategic optionality can outweigh capital-intensive infrastructure ownership.

    Recent findings suggest that ownership doesn’t equal control. Multicloud doesn’t equal resilience. Sovereignty doesn’t equal security. Capability doesn’t equal returns. Competitive advantage requires mastering these distinctions.

    By 2030, which enterprises will outperform?

    Sources indicate that 1. Enterprises owning the most infrastructure?

    Industry observers note that 2. Enterprises purchasing compute at the lowest price?

    Industry observers note that 3. Enterprises architecting the freedom to operate across changing technological, economic and geopolitical situations?

    My conviction favors the third scenario, provided freedom is measurable, tested and economically sustainable.

    The next phase of infrastructure reset isn’t simply about where intelligence runs. It’s about whether enterprises retain their authority, resilience and economic capacity to act decisively when the operating conditions change.

    In a recent development, infrastructure will increasingly determine whether enterprise strategy creates sustainable business value. Will competitive advantage come from infrastructure ownership and lowest cost compute, or will it come from proven resilience, risk-adjusted enterprise economics and strategic freedom?​.

    Sources indicate that forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

    While much of the attention has gone to chipmakers in 2026, the artificial intelligence (AI) boom is creating some unexpected winners, and Micron Technology (MU -1.22%) just might be the next. As models grow more demanding and data centers continue to expand, the need for advanced memory will only accelerate.

    Plus, with several major trends working in its favor, this memory stock could turn out to be one of 2027's biggest AI beneficiaries.

    Micron is emerging as one of the most notable suppliers to the AI build-out, providing the dynamic random access memory (DRAM), NAND, and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) needed to power AI infrastructure. In fact, its fiscal 2026 performance showed how dramatically that position has driven he organization's growth, with its cloud and data center products benefiting from strong demand and improved pricing.

    Sources indicate that at the same time, the tech giant says AI demand for memory is growing faster than the industry can expand supply. To that end, Micron has increasingly focused on higher-value data center products, where demand for HBM and advanced server memory is being driven by hyperscaler spending. Indeed, advanced AI chips require enormous amounts of HBM memory to move data efficiently.

    NASDAQ · As of 9:52 AM ET 11/17/26.

    Meanwhile, the firm has been expanding its portfolio as AI systems become more complex and demanding. For example, its recent product developments include advanced server memory, high-performance solid-state drives (SSDs) designed for AI workloads, and new memory products for physical AI applications.

    Looking ahead, Micron is heading into fiscal 2027 with management pointing to continued AI-driven demand, while its latest guidance and product roadmap suggest that advanced data center memory remains central to its growth strategy.

    According to recent reports, in fact, memory demand continues to accelerate even as bringing new supply online is neither quick nor easy. That very bottleneck is supporting stronger pricing and profitability across its business.

    Recent findings suggest that after all, building leading-edge manufacturing capacity takes years and requires enormous investment. Micron's own expansion aims are proof of that.

    Specifically, its new Idaho manufacturing capacity is expected to begin producing DRAM wafers in calendar 2027, while its larger New York expansion will help expand supply over the next 20-plus years.

    That combination could make Micron one of the more interesting AI stocks to watch in 2027. That's because, unlike companies whose valuations depend on future promises, Micron is already embedded in the AI infrastructure stack where supply constraints and customer demand are tangible.

    On top of that, the manufacturer is benefiting from its position as the only major U.S.-based memory manufacturer. Indeed, that's an important strategic advantage as governments and tech companies prioritize supply chain resilience and domestic manufacturing.

    But the manufacturer still faces meaningful risks.

    For one, Micron remains exposed to the cyclicality of the memory industry. In other words, if AI spending slows or manufacturers bring too much newly introduced capacity online, memory prices could come under pressure.

    Plus, there's the risk that hyperscalers may not earn attractive enough returns on their AI investments. That means any slowdown in data center construction would likely affect Micron's revenue outlook.

    Industry observers note that right now, 45 of 49 Wall Street analysts rate Micron stock a buy or strong buy, with an average target price of $1,561.91, suggesting the stock could more than double by this time next year. On top of that, its forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 4.5 offers an attractive entry point for investors who think the AI memory boom still has room to run. The combination of upside and low valuation could help Micron outperform AI peers in 2027.

    Looking ahead, with memory becoming increasingly vital to the AI build-out and Micron strengthening its market position, the company could surprise investors as one of 2027's biggest AI stock winners.

    Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron (CVX) is the first dividend pick. Earlier this month, the firm paid a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share. At an annualized dividend of $7.12 per share, CVX offers a dividend yield of about 3.5%.

    Recent findings suggest that after a meeting with senior leadership, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on CVX and raised his price target to $240 from $225. Among the key takeaways Mehta emphasized was that Chevron is building a solid pipeline of promising international exploration projects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa and the Eastern Mediterranean. In particular, he mentioned the focus on Venezuela, where Chevron expects to more than double gross production to 600 kbd from about 280 kbd by 2031, using three joint ventures.

    In a recent development, mehta also noted Chevron's efforts to deploy fresh technologies, especially in shale and tight-oil operations. CVX is focused on boosting productivity and efficiency to maximize free cash flow, he added.

    Sources indicate that initiatives such as artificial lift optimization, AI and machine learning, and advanced chemical treatments are expected to improve recovery by about 10% in newly introduced wells. Consequently, capital spending per barrel in U.S. shale is projected to fall 25% in 2026, with total Permian spending dropping below $3.5 billion.

    Mehta also noted that Chevron sees power as a growth opportunity and is using its U.S. natural gas portfolio, key equipment and partnerships to meet rising demand. Notably, Chevron recently signed a 20-year power purchase deal with Microsoft (MSFT) to supply 2.67 GW of behind-the-meter capacity. This project, called Kilby, is expected to see its first power delivery in 2028 and generate mid-teens returns and long-term cash flows.

With a quarterly cash distribution of 56 cents per common unit ($2.24 per common unit annualized), EPD offers a yield of about 6%.

    Following a recent call with the tech giant, RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on EPD with a price target of $42. The analyst slightly lowered her estimates for the second half of 2026, citing margin and volume normalization, though demand dynamics remain strong.

    Recent findings suggest that while the 5-star analyst expects a sequential decline due to normal seasonality and normalization following high spreads in the first half of the year, she still expects EPD to report another solid quarter (Q3 2026) and enter 2027 with a favorable setup. Ahead of Q3 earnings, Scotto expects investors to focus on export demand durability, EPD's ability to profit from spot cargo sales and growth in Permian volumes.

    Scotto continues to expect $150 million of common unit buybacks per quarter in the second half of 2026. She expects buybacks to increase to $200 million per quarter in 2027, as capex spending declines and free cash flow improves.

    According to recent reports, in total, Scotto is bullish on EPD and views it as a core MLP holding that has both offensive and defensive characteristics. The analyst praised EPD's diverse asset base as ensuring stable cash flows. "Furthermore, the partnership's multi-year organic growth backlog helps provide visibility on long-term distribution growth," Scotto noted.

    Industry News: What Happens To Your Premium Domains When You Pass Away?

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (746 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that michael Gargiulo, CEO of VPN,com.
    • ​Some families inherit real estate, investment portfolios and businesses when a loved one passes away.
    • It has been revealed that as a domain advisor and expert, I have spent the better part of the past decade working with owners of previous domains and various entities that understand how valuable digital real estate is today.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that michael Gargiulo, CEO of VPN,com. We help Fortune 1000, entrepreneurs and companies protect their brand.

    ​Some families inherit real estate, investment portfolios and businesses when a loved one passes away. Others inherit domain names potentially worth millions of dollars without knowing what they own, what those assets are worth or how to protect them.

    It has been revealed that as a domain advisor and expert, I have spent the better part of the past decade working with owners of previous domains and various entities that understand how valuable digital real estate is today. One overlooked situation is what to do with these valuable assets after the owner passes away.

    Industry observers note that for example, consider a successful businessperson who owns a substantially valued domain in the seven-figure realm, but the registration is tethered to their personal accountant. What’s more, all notices, like renewals, are routed to a private email address. In this situation, nobody really knows what to do should the owner suddenly pass away.

    The problem isn’t necessarily inheritance; it’s the absence of a plan to preserve what was inherited.

    Premium domains are more than website addresses. They hold value because they can represent brand recognition, customer trust, intellectual property-related value and significant commercial opportunities. In truth, protecting your domain is comparable to measures you might take to protect your own estate.

    It has been revealed that even a domain that was acquired in the past for a nominal investment could vest and be worth a lot more in the present day. Short.com, for example, might garner interest from multiple parties, and established domains could be the centerpiece for the right company.

    While some owners may carefully document their property, investments and bank accounts, they often leave their domain portfolios out of their estate planning entirely. An oversight like this can swiftly become expensive if you don’t plan properly in advance, while you are still alive.

    Much like any tangible asset, domains shouldn’t be overlooked in succession planning. Preparing in advance means having the right documentation in place now. It means assessing inventory and defining domain value. It also means keeping careful tabs on access information, renewals, certifications and access.

    After you have these credentials in order, your best plan of action is to work with an experienced estate attorney. They can use their expertise to assess your individual circumstances and create a strong plan that protects your assets into the future against the unknown.

    Along the way, discuss key elements like access planning, credential management and who can access this information if the unthinkable occurs. This also means protecting these assets, securing important access information and ensuring ongoing obligations, such as fees and renewals, are handled accordingly.

    In a recent development, domains have value and are digital real estate that can increase in value over time. Knowing this beforehand can help heirs capture the full value, even if they are unfamiliar with how domaining works. For example, a domain valuation may show $50,000, but the domain may be worth more because it offers strategic value to a growing brand. Ensure your assigned legal counsel and trustees understand the potential buyer market by properly documenting your domain now.

    It has been revealed that not every inherited domain should be sold. Some may provide ongoing business value. Others may benefit from being held until market conditions improve. Certain portfolios may be better managed or sold through experienced professional representation.

    The best advice I can offer is to blueprint for the asset, not necessarily its sale. This is because many domains can be held in a portfolio and continue to accrue in value over time. As market conditions improve, it’s beneficial to have experienced professionals manage the portfolio and know when to hold and when to sell.

    Of course, the right decision depends on the asset, the beneficiaries’ objectives, the estate’s financial obligations and the commercial opportunities involved. Forward-thinking owners can make those decisions easier by documenting their intentions while they’re alive. Identify which domains support operating businesses, which are long-term investments, and which might reasonably be sold.

    A valuable domain can outlive its founder. This is why it’s so crucial to protect its value in advance. Doing so, however, requires a plan made with qualified financial and legal experts that survives the person who built it.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that investors often look to Bank of America (BAC +0.06%) and JPMorgan Chase (JPM -1.05%) when seeking stability. These banking titans dominate the financial landscape, but choosing the better buy for 2027 requires a closer look.

    Bank of America focuses on a balance of consumer banking and wealth management while maintaining a vast digital footprint. JPMorgan Chase operates as a global financial powerhouse with unparalleled scale across investment banking and retail services. This comparison evaluates their financial health, growth trajectories, and valuation to determine which better fits your long-term goals.

    According to recent reports, bank of America offers a wide range of financial services across segments such as consumer banking, wealth management, and global markets. Among diversified bank stocks, it at the moment serves roughly 69 million consumer and small business clients across more than 35 countries. Its strategy focuses on digital integration, operating approximately 3,500 retail financial centers and 15,000 ATMs to maintain local presence while expanding its online capabilities.

    Reliable recent quarterly figures for at least one of these companies aren't available, so this comparison uses each company's latest full fiscal year. In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $113.1 billion, representing growth of roughly 6.8% over the previous year. The company reported net income of approximately $30.5 billion, resulting in a net margin of close to 27%.

    In a recent development, as of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 1.2, calculated by dividing total debt by shareholder equity. The current ratio stood at approximately 0.4, and free cash flow for the year reached nearly $12.6 billion. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 31.7% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

    JPMorgan Chase is a global financial leader serving millions of individual customers, corporations, and governments across more than 100 markets. The firm operates through major segments including consumer and community banking, the commercial and investment bank, and asset and wealth management. Its scale is extensive, with the Chase brand providing national coverage through more than 5,000 branches across the 48 contiguous states.

    In fiscal 2025, the bank generated revenue of approximately $182.4 billion, representing nearly 2.8% growth over the prior year. Net income reached close to $57 billion for the same period. This resulted in a net margin of roughly 31.3%, showing the amount of revenue that remained as profit after all expenses.

    In a recent development, as of JPMorgan's December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 2.6, illustrating that the firm uses more debt relative to its equity than its peer. The current ratio was roughly 0.5, and free cash flow for the fiscal year 2025 was nearly negative $147.8 billion. Free cash flow represents cash from operations minus capital expenditures, showing the surplus cash available after maintaining operations.

    It has been revealed that bank of America deals with significant regulatory and legal risks, highlighted by a December 2024 consent order regarding its anti-money laundering compliance. The company is also managing ongoing securities fraud class action lawsuits with deadlines extending into late 2026. Market instability and competition from other large institutions like Morgan Stanley (MS +0.14%) also pressure the bank's long-term outlook.

    Industry observers note that JPMorgan Chase faces legal and regulatory risks, including ongoing investigations and a cash sweep lawsuit that was partially allowed to proceed in early 2026. Credit risk remains a factor, particularly given concentrations in industries such as commercial real estate, alongside operational risks posed by emerging technologies. The company competes intensely with major rivals such as Wells Fargo (WFC -0.28%) to maintain its dominant market position.

    Bank of America appears to be the more value-oriented choice, trading at a lower multiple of both its future earnings estimates and its book value.

    Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

    According to recent reports, the forward P/E compares a stock price to its future earnings estimates over the next year. The P/B ratio compares the stock price with the company's book value (its assets minus its liabilities, roughly what shareholders would own on paper), and investors lean on it for insurers and banks. A lower P/B ratio means the stock costs less relative to book value.

    I think these two stocks are pretty conservative investments. It's obviously not impossible for banks to blow up, but these are massive, established institutions, and they've been bailed out by the U.S. government before. So, in that sense, they strike me as relatively safe investments.

    In a recent development, bank of America's recent revenue growth was stronger, but JPMorgan has a higher net margin. Bank of America's dividend yields more, but on an absolute basis, JPMorgan's payout is higher.

    Let's see how both stocks have performed:.

    It has been revealed that bank of America badly trails JPMorgan, but more importantly, the former hasn't even kept pace with the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.17%). The whole point of investing in individual stocks is to beat the market's average return. B of A is not making a strong argument for itself here.

    Industry observers note that past performance, of course, is no indication of future results. The next 10 years may look very different than the past. But if I'm buying a bank stock for 2027 and beyond, JPMorgan gets my vote.

    #15945. ​AI's Hidden Cost: When Organizational Debt Comes Due

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1010 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    ​AI's Hidden Cost: When Organizational Debt Comes Due

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1010 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Luboslava Uram is COO and CTO at Solvd Group, a subsidiary of Allianz Group.
    • ​For decades, technology leaders have managed technical debt: outdated systems, accumulated exceptions, architectural shortcuts and temporary solutions that somehow became permanent.
    • Industry observers note that today, I believe artificial intelligence is exposing another kind of debt—one that is potentially harder to resolve because it does not sit in our technology architecture: organizational debt.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Luboslava Uram is COO and CTO at Solvd Group, a subsidiary of Allianz Group. Transforming the claim management experience.

    ​For decades, technology leaders have managed technical debt: outdated systems, accumulated exceptions, architectural shortcuts and temporary solutions that somehow became permanent.

    Industry observers note that today, I believe artificial intelligence is exposing another kind of debt—one that is potentially harder to resolve because it does not sit in our technology architecture: organizational debt. It accumulates through unclear responsibilities, duplicated processes, conflicting performance objectives, inconsistent data and decisions that require coordination across multiple organizational layers. Most enterprises have learned to operate despite these inefficiencies. People compensate for them every day.​.

    But what happens when AI agents must navigate processes that were never clearly defined in the first place?​.

    Throughout my career leading technology platforms and global operations, I have observed how remarkably good people are at making imperfect organizations work. For example:.

    • A process officially belongs to one department, but everyone knows that unusual cases require calling an experienced colleague on another team.

    • Three systems contain different versions of the same information, but someone knows which number to trust.

    • Two functions share responsibility for an outcome, yet experienced managers understand who actually makes the final decision.​.

    These arrangements become part of how organizations operate. They rarely appear in process documentation or technology architecture. Imagine introducing an AI agent into that environment. Which information should it trust? Which process should it follow? Who can authorize an exception? Who is accountable?

    For a human employee, years of experience and informal relationships often resolve these uncertainties. For an AI agent, they must become explicit. Research supports the significance of this challenge. McKinsey’s July 2026 analysis, “The Operating Model Advantage“ (registration required), reported that only 21% of surveyed companies had fundamentally redesigned their operating models around AI. We are introducing increasingly sophisticated technology into organizations that have barely changed how they operate.​.

    I see three areas where accumulated organizational debt becomes particularly visible.​.

    Industry observers note that almost every AI transformation eventually encounters the same obstacle: Data is incomplete, inconsistent or unreliable. The immediate reaction is usually technological. Build better pipelines, clean databases or introduce another data platform. But why did the problem arise?

    In a recent development, often, different functions maintain competing definitions, nobody owns data quality across the entire process and business knowledge remains disconnected from operational records. PwC’s “2026 Digital Trends in Operations Survey“ found that 87% of surveyed operations leaders reported poor data quality affecting the value achieved from digital initiatives. Technology can correct individual data problems. But unless accountability for business meaning, quality and maintenance changes, those problems may return. The question is not only whether data is AI-ready. It is also who is responsible for keeping it AI-ready.​.

    In complex organizations, one team analyzes information, another recommends an action, a third owns the process and someone else approves the decision. People navigate these structures through meetings, escalations and negotiations. AI agents introduce a different challenge. If an agent can recommend or execute an action, who has authorized that authority? Which decisions remain human? Who can override an automated action? Who owns its consequences?

    IBM’s June 2026 research among technology executives highlighted this accountability gap: Approximately “two-thirds of surveyed CIOs and CTOs report being held accountable for AI systems they do not fully control.” As AI moves from assisting people toward executing operational decisions, unclear accountability becomes increasingly difficult to manage.​.

    Consider a customer journey involving operations, finance and customer service. Operations targets faster processing. Finance prioritizes lower costs. Customer service focuses on satisfaction. Each objective makes sense individually. But optimizing one can damage another. Experienced managers constantly negotiate these trade-offs.

    It has been revealed that what happens when AI begins optimizing decisions at machine speed? Without clear priorities, an agent might reduce processing time while increasing rework or minimize immediate costs while creating more expensive consequences later. AI can optimize what we tell it to measure. Leadership must decide what is actually worth optimizing.​.

    I do not believe organizations should spend years redesigning everything before introducing AI. That would simply create another transformation program with uncertain outcomes. Instead, I would use AI implementation as an opportunity to resolve organizational debt where it matters most. Start with one significant end-to-end process and take four practical steps.​.

    Industry observers note that 1. Make ownership explicit. Identify one accountable owner for the overall business outcome, even when execution spans multiple functions.

    2. Establish trusted business context. Agree on data definitions, authoritative sources and responsibility for keeping information reliable.

    3. Clarify decision authority. Define which decisions AI can support, which actions it may execute and where human judgement or approval remains necessary.

    4. Align performance measures. Evaluate the complete customer or operational outcome, not simply the productivity of individual activities.​.

    It has been revealed that only then should the organization determine which work to automate and how to introduce AI agents. This approach does not eliminate every complexity. But it prevents organizations from automating problems they should have resolved first.​.

    For years, enterprises have absorbed organizational complexity through additional coordination, management layers, manual interventions and experienced employees who understand how things really work. That approach has a cost, even when it remains invisible in technology budgets.

    Sources indicate that AI presents an opportunity to challenge it. The most valuable AI transformation may not be the one that automates the greatest number of tasks. It may be the one that finally eliminates unnecessary handovers, resolves conflicting responsibilities and makes better decisions possible across the business.

    This is why I increasingly see AI transformation as an organizational leadership challenge, not simply a technology initiative.​.

    We should stop asking only how to make AI work within our organizations and start asking what needs to change in our organizations for AI to work effectively. The debt has been accumulating for years. AI is simply making the bill harder to ignore.​​​.

    Industry News: This Magnificent Growth Stock Just Entered the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Cloud Race, and It Looks Dirt Cheap

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Singapore-based Sea Limited (SE -1.72%) operates the largest e-commerce platform in Southeast Asia, in addition to a booming digital financial services business and a mobile game development studio that owns some of the world's most popular titles.
    • But Sea just announced a brand-newly introduced business called Sea Cloud, which will offer a range of artificial intelligence (AI) services to enterprise customers.
    • Sea stock is currently the cheapest it has ever been by one widely used valuation metric, and in fact, it's trading at a steep discount to most other AI cloud stocks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Singapore-based Sea Limited (SE -1.72%) operates the largest e-commerce platform in Southeast Asia, in addition to a booming digital financial services business and a mobile game development studio that owns some of the world's most popular titles.

    But Sea just announced a brand-newly introduced business called Sea Cloud, which will offer a range of artificial intelligence (AI) services to enterprise customers. The firm is uniquely positioned to make this venture a success, and it could result in significant long-term returns for investors.

    Sea stock is currently the cheapest it has ever been by one widely used valuation metric, and in fact, it's trading at a steep discount to most other AI cloud stocks. Read on.

    Shopee is Sea's hybrid business-to-consumer and consumer-to-consumer e-commerce platform, and it has a dominant presence in Southeast Asian countries like Indonesia, Malaysia, and Singapore. Shopee processed 4.5 billion orders worth a combined $39.7 billion during the recent third quarter of 2026 (ended Sept. 30) alone, with those figures growing by 25% and 23% year over year, respectively.

    Industry observers note that then there is Monee, Sea's digital financial services platform. It offers buy now, pay later loans to consumers to boost their purchasing power, and it also lends money to Shopee merchants to help them grow their businesses. It had 44 million active borrowers during the third quarter, and its loan book grew by a whopping 60% to $12.6 billion.

    Over the last two years, Sea has invested heavily in AI capabilities to make those platforms more efficient. The manufacturer is now running AI software at scale in areas like fraud detection, customer service, and content generation, and it has mastered the art of squeezing the most value out of data center computing hardware.

    In a recent development, developing those capabilities cost Sea a lot of money, but it will start profiting off them by offering them to enterprise customers through Sea Cloud. Unlike most other cloud providers, Sea's strategy won't involve building expensive data centers unless specifically requested by customers, with prepayments attached.

    Industry observers note that in fact, Sea is entering the AI cloud race with a rock-solid balance sheet. It boasts a whopping $9.5 billion in cash (and cash equivalents) with under $1 billion in debt, whereas many other companies in this space have borrowed truckloads of money with an uncertain path to profitability.

    NYSE · As of 9:52 AM ET 11/17/26.

    Recent findings suggest that the Sea Cloud business is still in the formation stage, so it hasn't generated any revenue just yet. But even without it, Sea delivered $8.6 billion in revenue from its existing businesses during the third quarter, up by an eye-popping 43.4% from the year-ago period. It blew away Wall Street's average forecast of $8.1 billion.

    Sea also delivered a great result at the bottom line, so its rapid revenue growth wasn't a result of burning through significant amounts of cash. It generated $931.3 million in adjusted (non-GAAP) earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA), up 28.6% from the year-ago period.

    Industry observers note that despite Sea's incredible operating results, its stock is actually down 40% this year. It's mainly because management floated the idea of spinning Monee off into a separate company, and investors are still unsure what the structure might look like. However, the deal will have to satisfy regulators in multiple countries, and Sea's chief executive Forrest Li claims the process could take up to three years, so nothing is set in stone just yet.

    Industry observers note that following its sharp decline, Sea stock is trading at a price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of just 1.5 as I write this on Nov. 15, which is the cheapest level in its history. Moreover, Sea is significantly cheaper than other AI cloud providers like CoreWeave, IREN, and Nebius Group.

    With a portfolio of highly successful existing businesses, a rock-solid balance sheet, and an incoming AI cloud platform, I think Sea stock could be a great long-term buy at the current level.

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (933 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    It’s Time To Extend Collective Defense To Consumers

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (933 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ravi Dhaval, Fortune 500 advisor & inventor of patent-pending (#19/440,089), quantum-powered AI platform for proactive global cyber defense.
    • It has been revealed that for years, executive security briefings have centered on one fear: machine-speed attacks powered by artificial intelligence (AI).
    • That gap is where I focused my published patent application, aiming to close it by simulating attack paths in real time, sharing threat intelligence without exposing raw data, and orchestrating defenses automatically.​.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ravi Dhaval, Fortune 500 advisor & inventor of patent-pending (#19/440,089), quantum-powered AI platform for proactive global cyber defense.

    It has been revealed that for years, executive security briefings have centered on one fear: machine-speed attacks powered by artificial intelligence (AI). Boards fund automated response, AI red teaming and zero-trust policies to protect the corporate perimeter. Yet most cyber defense remains reactive, built on detection after the fact and limited by classical computing’s difficulty simulating complex attack paths.

    That gap is where I focused my published patent application, aiming to close it by simulating attack paths in real time, sharing threat intelligence without exposing raw data, and orchestrating defenses automatically.​.

    In a recent development, the more unsettling reality sits outside the boardroom. While Fortune 500 companies harden their defenses, everyday people face AI-native attacks aimed at their finances and personal data, with nothing comparable protecting them. Everyday life has become the primary attack surface.

    In a recent development, indirect prompt injection hides instructions in content an AI system later reads and obeys, and OWASP ranks prompt injection the top risk for applications built on large language models. One of the newest delivery methods is the poisoned instruction file. In October 2026, researchers at Forever Security reported finding a malicious AGENTS.md file, disguised as engineering notes, in a customer’s downloads folder, which is the one folder a website can write to without a click. AI coding agents such as OpenAI Codex and Claude Code follow the instruction files in whatever folder they open, so the planted text behaved like a program while slipping past every control built for executables. In testing, it led agents to rewrite their own configuration, opening the door to malware installation and stolen login tokens.

    According to recent reports, voice and video impersonation is another growing threat. The FBI warns that criminals use generative AI to clone the voices of loved ones and to produce convincing video for live calls. The FTC notes a scammer needs only a short audio clip, which can often be pulled from content posted online.

    The growing list of connected devices in the home adds still more exposure. Thermostats, smart TVs, voice assistants and even light bulbs all exchange data. The FBI cautions that one unsecured IoT device can give an attacker a path into the home router and everything behind it.

    It has been revealed that this holiday season, many consumers will install shopping agents: AI deal finders and checkout assistants that request access to email, saved cards and sometimes even password managers. OWASP calls this excessive agency, meaning an AI holding more permission than its task requires. A hidden instruction in a fake review or poisoned listing could steer such an agent into leaking credentials or placing fraudulent orders.

    It has been revealed that antivirus software and firewalls hunt for malicious signatures and binaries. A natural-language instruction, a cloned voice or an edited settings file is none of those. As the Forever researchers argue, nearly every defense we rely on assumes a human who clicks, approves or runs the code. Once an agent takes the human’s place, that assumption breaks. Asking the public to fight AI attacks with tools from an earlier era invites systemic failure.

    Businesses have a system for defending one another, but the public doesn’t. Since Presidential Decision Directive 63 in 1998, Information Sharing and Analysis Centers (ISACs) have let critical-infrastructure sectors pool threat intelligence and defend collectively.

    Recent findings suggest that consumers can report to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center or the FTC, but those channels exist to support investigations after the fact. None of them pools what one household experiences into protection for the next one in real time.

    Industry observers note that the biggest gap needs a latest institution: Consumer ISACs that collect telemetry on consumer-targeted AI attacks and voice-cloning operations and turn it into protective updates for home gateways and phones. Natural members are ISPs, mobile carriers, device makers and AI platforms, the companies already standing between consumers and attackers. CISA would be the federal partner, mirroring how sector ISACs pair industry operators with government. Privacy is the hard part, but solvable. In my patent application’s federated design, for instance, I chose to pair secure enclaves with threshold cryptography so that no single party ever holds the full decryption key.

    It has been revealed that public health relies on clean-water infrastructure, not purification tablets in every home. Similarly, internet providers should build behavioral analytics into residential gateways to protect devices that can’t run security software of their own. The attack-path modeling that enterprise platforms are beginning to use, which maps every route an intruder could take and ranks the most damaging, could inform simpler gateway logic that spots and blocks an intruder moving between smart devices.

    Consumer AI tools should ship with least-privilege permissions and require explicit human approval before touching credentials or payments. Because no single control reliably stops prompt injection, protections must be layered. Vendors should also disclose which models, plug-ins and data connections their agents can reach.

    Share these steps with your employees:.

    Sources indicate that corporate defenses are only as strong as the exposed public around them. We built collective defense for pipelines and power grids. It is time to build it for people, and consumer ISACs are where security leaders can start. Leadership will be measured not only by how well we protect balance sheets, but by how effectively we advocate for everyone else’s digital safety.​.

Looking ahead, with newly introduced growth opportunities emerging across advertising and e-commerce, here's why investors might consider buying this retail giant before the new year and holding it forever.

    The latest increase brought the organization's annual dividend to $0.99 per share, up from $0.94 in the previous fiscal year, just as it's done for the past 53 years.

    Industry observers note that but Walmart's dividend history is about more than returning cash to shareholders. It's proof of something more vital: the durability of its business, as Walmart is built around supplying necessities at competitive prices, regardless of whether the economy is booming or slowing.

    NASDAQ · As of 9:58 AM ET 11/17/26.

    On top of that, its enormous scale, established customer relationships, and extensive distribution network make it difficult for competitors to replicate what it has built. Instead of relying on its traditional retail business, Walmart has spent years expanding into faster-growing areas that could support decades of future growth.

    Retail has traditionally been a relatively low-margin business. Walmart moves enormous volumes of products, but selling groceries and household essentials leaves limited room for profit growth. That's why growing advertising and membership businesses have become increasingly key.

    From there, it's crucial to consider Walmart Connect, the company's advertising platform. Since Walmart has direct relationships with millions of shoppers and access to valuable shopping data, it can offer brands opportunities to reach consumers much closer to the point of purchase.

    In fact, that strategy is already driving growth.

    Walmart's global advertising business grew 38% in the second quarter of fiscal 2027, while its U.S. advertising business grew 43%, excluding VIZIO. Plus, the acquisition of VIZIO gives Walmart an opportunity to expand its advertising reach into connected television, creating another channel where it can monetize customer relationships.

    Meanwhile, memberships offer another opportunity. For example, Walmart+ and Sam's Club memberships encourage repeat purchases while creating recurring fee revenue.

    Plus, they give customers more reasons to consolidate their shopping with Walmart rather than spending across several retailers. With that, global membership fee revenue rose 17% in the second quarter of fiscal 2027.

    Meanwhile, beyond advertising and memberships, Walmart is expanding globally to drive the next phase of its growth.

    Industry observers note that these days, Walmart's growth isn't limited to the U.S. In fact, the company operates across multiple international markets, including Mexico, Canada, China, India, and several countries in Central America and Africa. These businesses provide exposure to different markets and give Walmart more opportunities to expand.

    According to recent reports, on top of that, its international strategy opens up opportunities in digital markets. In India, for instance, Walmart has a significant stake in Flipkart, one of the country's major e-commerce platforms. As India's digital economy and consumer markets expand, it offers a long-term opportunity that's difficult to replicate through traditional U.S. retail operations.

    Likewise, Sam's Club is another vital part of this opportunity, as its membership-based warehouse model generates recurring revenue and encourages customer loyalty and repeat spending. In particular, the format is seeing significant potential in markets such as China and Mexico, where membership growth and digital adoption can support expansion.

    Still, investors should weigh that growth potential against the stock's valuation and risks.

    The vast majority of Wall Street analysts covering the stock rate it a buy or strong buy, with an average price target of $131.45. These days, the stock trades at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of about 38, so many investors are already expecting meaningful growth. Still, Walmart's strong competitive position and growth opportunities help justify that premium.

    According to recent reports, that said, owning Walmart isn't without risks. For one, its enormous size makes growth challenging, while competition from other retailers could pressure margins and market share. Despite that, Walmart's staying power comes from sticking to the business model that has sustained it for decades, while finding new ways to grow and adapt.

    In a recent development, ultimately, Walmart has spent 53 consecutive years proving it can continue to reward shareholders. Looking ahead, with e-commerce, advertising, and memberships creating newly introduced opportunities, its growth runway is far from over. And that's why investors might consider buying shares before the new year and holding them for life.
